Giza governorate is one of the governorates in Egypt. It is in the center of the country, on the west side of the Nile River, opposite Cairo. The capital of Giza governorate is the city of Giza. It includes land along the Nile Valley around Giza and part of Egypt's western desert, including the Bahariya Oasis. On April 14, 2011, it also included the 6th of October governorate. The Giza governorate is famous for the Great Sphinx and the Pyramids of Giza.

José Vitor Roque Jr., born on August 31, 1976, in Santa Rita do Sapucaí, is known as Roque Júnior. He was a football player who played as a defender. He last played for Ituano Futebol Clube. Roque Júnior played 48 times for the Brazil national team. He was part of the team that won the 2002 World Cup.

In computer architecture, 64-bit data units, like integers and memory addresses, are made up of 64 bits or 8 bytes. Similarly, 64-bit CPUs and ALUs use registers, address buses, or data buses that are 64 bits wide. 64-bit microcomputers use 64-bit microprocessors. From a software perspective, 64-bit computing involves using code with 64-bit virtual memory addresses. However, not all 64-bit instruction sets support full 64-bit virtual memory; for example, x86-64 and ARMv8 use only 48 bits, requiring the remaining 16 bits to be all zeros or all ones. 64-bit processors have been used in supercomputers since the 1970s, in workstations and servers since the early 1990s, and in mainstream personal computers since 2003, with the introduction of x86-64 and PowerPC G5 processors. In 2012, 64-bit processors were used in ARM architecture for smartphones and tablets, starting with the iPhone 5s in 2013. A 64-bit register can hold over 18 quintillion values. The range of values that can be stored in 64 bits depends on how the number is represented. In binary, it can hold numbers from 0 to 18,446,744,073,709,551,615. In two's complement, it can hold numbers from -9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,807. A 64-bit computer can access 2 bytes, or 16 exabytes, of memory directly. Generally, a 64-bit computer architecture has 64-bit wide integer and address processor registers, supporting 64-bit data types and addresses. However, a CPU may have different external data or address buses, even larger than the register size. The term can also refer to the size of low-level data types, like 64-bit floating-point numbers.
La Chapelle is a town in the Allier region of central France.

Gorno is a town in the Mosea region. It is in the part of Switzerland where people speak Italian. This area is in the canton of Graubünden. On January 1, 2017, the towns of Leggia and Verdabbio became one town called Gorno.

La Riviera is a census-designated place in Sacramento County, California, United States. It is part of the Sacramento–Arden-Arcade–Roseville metropolitan area. The population was 10,802 in 2010, up from 10,273 in 2000. La Riviera is mainly a residential neighborhood. It is located between the American River to the north and Highway 50 to the south.

Glenn Franklin Howerton III, born on April 13, 1976, is an American actor. He was born in Japan. Glenn is known for his role as Dennis Reynolds in the TV show "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia." He also writes for and is an executive producer of this show. Glenn played Jack Griffin in "A.P. Bio." He also starred as the main character in a short-lived sitcom called "That '80s Show."

Birdbrook is a small village and civil parish in Essex, England. It is southeast of Haverhill, Suffolk. Birdbrook is about 34 kilometers (21 miles) north of Chelmsford, the county town. The village is part of the Braintree district and the Saffron Walden parliamentary constituency. Birdbrook is part of the Bumpsteads and Upper Colne parish cluster. It is 93 meters above sea level. In 2011, the village had 397 people living there. There is a pub called "The Plough" and a church named "St Augustine of Canterbury." Nearby is Moyns Park, a Grade I listed Elizabethan country house. It's said that Ian Fleming finished his novel "From Russia, With Love" there.

The Strategic Defense Initiative (SDI) was a plan to protect the United States from nuclear missile attacks. It was first talked about on March 23, 1983, by President Ronald Reagan. He wanted scientists and engineers to develop a system to make nuclear weapons less important. In 1984, the Strategic Defense Initiative Organization (SDIO) was created to manage the project. Many new weapon ideas, like lasers and space-based systems, were studied, along with sensors and computers. During the late 1980s, some of these ideas were tested. Even today, some of the efforts continue. Under SDIO, Dr. James Isonson led the science and technology office. The focus was on basic research at labs, universities, and companies, which helped research in physics, supercomputing, and other fields. In 1987, the American Physical Society said that the technology was not ready yet and more research was needed. The SDI budget was cut. By the late 1980s, the focus shifted to the "Brilliant Pebbles" concept, which used small orbiting missiles to protect against attacks. These were cheaper to develop and use. SDI was controversial and some people worried it might start a new arms race. With the end of the Cold War in the early 1990s, support for SDI fell. It officially ended in 1993, when the focus changed to protecting against shorter-range missiles, and the agency was renamed the Ballistic Missile Defense Organization (BMDO).

Micheal Joseph Mansfield (March 16, 1903 – October 5, 2001) was an American politician and diplomat. He was a member of the Democratic Party and served as a US representative from 1943 to 1953, and as a US senator from 1953 to 1977. He was the longest-serving Senate Majority Leader, serving from 1961 to 1977. During his time as leader, he helped pass the Great Society programs and later criticized the Vietnam War as a mistake. Born in Brooklyn, he grew up in Great Falls, Montana. During World War I, he pretended to be older to join the US Navy. After the war, he taught history and political science at the University of Montana. He was elected to the House of Representatives and served on the House Committee on Foreign Affairs during World War II. In 1952, he won a Senate seat by defeating the Republican incumbent, Zales Ecton. He was Senate Majority Whip from 1957 to 1961. After Senator Lyndon B. Johnson became Vice President, Mansfield became Majority Leader. In the later years of his leadership, he opposed increasing involvement in the Vietnam War and supported President Richard Nixon's plan to use more Vietnamese soldiers instead. After leaving the Senate in 1977, Mansfield was appointed as the US Ambassador to Japan, a role he held until 1988. He was given the Presidential Medal of Freedom when he retired. Mansfield is the longest-serving US Ambassador to Japan. Later, he worked as a senior adviser on East Asian affairs for Goldman Sachs.

Jacques Marquette, a Jesuit missionary, was born on June 1, 1637, and died on May 18, 1675. He is sometimes known as Père Marquette or James Marquette. He was French and worked in America. Marquette helped found Michigan's first European settlement, called Sault Sainte Marie. Later, he founded St. Ignace, Michigan. In 1673, Marquette, along with Louis Jolliet, who was born near Quebec City, was the first European to explore and map the northern part of the Mississippi River valley.

Ruy Alexandre Guerra Coelho Pereira, born on August 22, 1931, is a film director and screenwriter from Portugal and Brazil. He was born in Lourenço Marques, which is now called Maputo, in Mozambique. At that time, Mozambique was still a Portuguese colony.

Tim Francis, born on May 1, 1928, and died on January 2, 2016, was a New Zealand diplomat. He served as the nation's permanent representative to the United Nations from 1978 to 1982. From 1988 to 1991, he was the ambassador to the United States. Between 1984 and 1988, he managed Tokelau.

Arthur Garfunkel, born on November 5, 1941, is an American singer, poet, and actor. He is most famous for singing with Paul Simon in the folk rock duo Simon & Garfunkel. His solo music highlights include several top hits and awards. Garfunkel won eight Grammy Awards, including a lifetime achievement award. Simon & Garfunkel were inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1990. In 2008, Garfunkel was ranked 86th on Rolling Stone's list of the 100 greatest singers of all time.

La Bañeza is a town in León, Castile and León, Spain. The 2010 census showed 11,050 people lived there. It's the capital of Tierra de La Bañeza. In the past, it was part of the Astur Conventus area during Roman times. The town was founded in the 9th century by Count Gatón from two villages, San Pedro de Périx, and Bani Eiza. In the late 19th century, a marquis lived there. In 1895, Queen Regent Maria Christina of Austria gave it city status. It has two important churches, San Salvador and Santa María. There are also celebrations like carnival, Holy Week, and August festivities. The August festival includes a motorcycle race called the La Bañeza Grand Prix. These events make the town popular for tourists.

Germanic languages belong to the Indo-European language family and are spoken by about 515 million people mainly in Europe, North America, Oceania, and Southern Africa. English, the most widely spoken Germanic language, has about 2 billion speakers. All Germanic languages come from a language called Proto-Germanic, which was spoken in Iron Age Scandinavia. West Germanic languages include English, with around 360 to 400 million native speakers; German, with over 100 million native speakers; and Dutch, with 24 million native speakers. Other West Germanic languages are Afrikaans, with over 7.1 million native speakers; Low German, considered separate dialects with about 0.3 million native speakers and up to 10 million people who can understand it; Yiddish, once used by about 13 million Jews in pre-World War II Europe, and Scots, both with 1.5 million native speakers; Limburgish varieties, with roughly 1.3 million speakers near the Dutch-German-Belgian border; and the Frisian languages, with over 0.5 million native speakers in the Netherlands and Germany. North Germanic languages include Danish, Norwegian, and Swedish, which are mutually intelligible and have about 20 million native speakers in the Nordic countries and an additional five million second-language speakers. These languages have been strongly influenced by West Germanic Middle Low German, with Low German words making up about 30 to 60 percent of their vocabularies. Other North Germanic languages are Faroese and Icelandic, which are more conservative with no significant Low German influence and more complex grammar. East Germanic languages, such as Gothic, Burgundian, and Vandalic, are now extinct. The last East Germanic language, Crimean Gothic, died off in the late 18th century. The Ethnologue lists 48 living Germanic languages, with 41 in the Western branch and six in the Northern branch. Riograndenser Hunsrückisch German is often considered a dialect, but is not categorized as such. German suffered a significant loss of "Sprachraum" after World War II, and many of its dialects are now dying out. Proto-Germanic, the common ancestor of all Germanic languages, was spoken around the middle of the 1st millennium BC in Iron Age Scandinavia. Early Germanic languages entered history when Germanic tribes moved south from Scandinavia in the 2nd century BC, settling in northern Germany and southern Denmark.
Millry is a town in Washington County, Alabama, United States. It became a town in 1947. In 2010, the population was 546. In 2000, there were 615 people.

György Sándor Ligeti (28 May 1923 – 12 June 2006) was a Hungarian-Austrian composer of contemporary classical music. He is known as one of the most important avant-garde composers in the second half of the 20th century and one of the most innovative and influential figures of his time. Born in Transylvania, Romania, he lived in Hungary before moving to Austria in 1956. He became an Austrian citizen in 1968. In 1973, he became a professor of composition at the Hamburg Hochschule für Musik und Theater, where he worked until 1989. Ligeti could only fully develop his avant-garde music style and new techniques after leaving Hungary in 1956. After working with electronic music in Cologne, his breakthrough came with works like "Atmosphères," where he used a technique he called micropolyphony. His later works moved away from chromaticism and towards polyrhythm. He is famous for his music being used in film soundtracks, even though he did not compose any film scores directly. Stanley Kubrick's films, especially "2001: A Space Odyssey," used Ligeti's music.

Durrës is the second largest city in Albania and the capital of its county. Situated on a flat plain near the southeastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, it has a Mediterranean climate. Founded by Greek colonists from Corinth and Corfu around 700 BC, it was called Epidamnos. Later known as Dyrrhachium, it became important during the Roman and Byzantine Empires. The Via Egnatia, a road from Rome to Constantinople, started in Durrës. During the Middle Ages, Durrës was controlled by Bulgaria, Venice, and the Ottoman Empire. After Albania became independent, Durrës was briefly the capital. It was then taken by Italy and Nazi Germany in the 1930s. During communism, Durrës grew in population and economy. Durrës has a big port that connects the city to Italy and other nearby countries. The most famous attraction is the Durrës Amphitheatre, which can hold up to 20,000 people and is the largest in the Balkan peninsula.

Raise Your Glass" is a song by American singer Pink. It is from her first greatest hits album "Greatest Hits... So Far!!" (2010). Pink wrote the song with Max Martin and Karl "Shellback" Schuster, and Martin and Schuster produced it. The song celebrates Pink's first decade as a performer, starting from 2000. It is dedicated to her fans. The song was released as the album's main single on October 5, 2010, by Jive Records. It was both popular and well-received, with most music critics praising it. The song became a hit, reaching the top ten in several countries, including the United States, where it was Pink's third number-one single. In 2011, "Raise Your Glass" was ranked number thirteen on the top 40 year-end chart based on Mediabase. The song was also used in a commercial for the 2011 movie "Bridesmaids" and in trailers for the films "What's Your Number?" and "New Year's Eve.

In the early years of independent Greece, from 1833 to 1836 and then from 1845 until 2010, prefectures were the main administrative units. They no longer exist and have been replaced by regional units. The United Nations calls them departments. Prefectures were the second level of local government. They were grouped into 13 regions or, before 1987, 10 departments. Prefectures were divided into provinces and included many communities and municipalities. In 1994, prefectures became self-governing. Elections for prefects started that year. By 2010, there were 51 prefectures, with Attica having four. Attica had over a third of the country’s population. There were also three super-prefectures. The Kallikratis reform, which began on January 1, 2011, abolished prefectures. Regional units replaced many of them, especially on the mainland, and took over their administrative tasks.
cotton is a commune in Calvados department, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France.

A listed building or structure is one that's on a special list kept by different organizations in England, Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland. In Ireland, buildings are checked for the National Inventory of Architectural Heritage, following rules from the Granada Convention. But, in Ireland, the preferred term is "protected structure." Without permission from the local planning authority, you can't tear down, expand, or change a listed building. For major changes to important buildings, a central government agency is consulted. In England and Wales, a national group must be told if any part of a listed building is being demolished. Some religious buildings in regular use can be exempt from this rule if their religious group has its own permission process. Building owners must sometimes fix and keep listed buildings in good condition, or they might face legal problems. Changes are allowed, but often, specific materials or methods are required. Besides buildings, other structures like bridges, statues, memorials, and even roads can be listed too. Ancient, military, or empty structures like Stonehenge are sometimes called scheduled monuments and protected by older laws. Cultural places like parks and gardens are sometimes listed, but not by law.

Ah, wilderness! It's a comedy by Eugene O'Neill, an American playwright. It was first shown on Broadway at the Guild Theatre on October 2, 1933. Unlike most of O'Neill's plays, this one has a happy ending. It also shows a happy family in early 1900s America. It's the only well-known comedy by O'Neill. The play was successful both in its first Broadway show and in the tours that followed. It is now a common choice for community theater.

Mark Dayton was born on January 26, 1947, in Minnesota. He became the 40th governor of Minnesota from 2011 to 2019. Before that, he was a U.S. senator for Minnesota from 2001 to 2007 and the Minnesota State Auditor from 1991 to 1995. Dayton belongs to the Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL). Dayton's great-grandfather, George Dayton, started a department store called Dayton's, which later became Target. After graduating from Yale University in 1969, Dayton worked as a teacher and social worker in New York City and Boston. He also worked as a legislative aide to U.S. Senator Walter Mondale and Minnesota Governor Rudy Perpich in the 1970s. In 1978, Dayton became the Minnesota Economic Development Commissioner. He married Alida Rockefeller Messinger in the same year. In 1982, Dayton tried to become a U.S. senator but lost. He returned to work for the Perpich administration until 1990, when he was elected Minnesota State Auditor. In 1998, Dayton tried to become governor but lost. He was elected to the U.S. Senate in 2000, defeating Republican Rod Grams. As a senator, he voted against the Iraq War and introduced a bill for a Department of Peace. In 2010, Dayton became governor again, defeating Republican Tom Emmer. He won a second term in 2014. Dayton left office in January 2019. While governor, he supported same-sex marriage and helped build U.S. Bank Stadium for the Minnesota Vikings.

In music theory, a theoretical key or impossible key has a key signature with at least one double-flat or double-sharp. Double-flats and double-sharps are usually used as accidentals. However, when placed in the key signature in music that uses equal temperament, the music becomes hard to read.

Samurai Champloo is a Japanese anime series made by Manglobe. The main people who worked on it were Shinichirō Watanabe, Kazuto Nakazawa, and Mahiro Maeda. This was Watanabe’s first time directing an anime TV show after making the popular Cowboy Beepop. It first aired on Fuji TV in Japan on May 20, 2004, and ended on March 19, 2005, after 26 episodes. Samurai Champloo is set in a different version of Japan from the 1600s to 1860s, with a mix of old and modern elements, especially hip-hop music. The story follows three characters: Mugen, a wild swordsman; Jin, a serious samurai; and Fuu, a brave girl looking for a samurai who smells like sunflowers. She asks them to join her on her journey across Japan. Samurai Champloo is similar to Watanabe’s other work, Cowboy Beepop. Both series are well-liked and mix different types of stories. They also use current music. The series was translated into English and released in North America by Geneon Entertainment, and later by Funimation. It was also released in the United Kingdom by MVM Films and in Australia and New Zealand by Madman Entertainment.

The Panhard VBL, also known as VBL, is a French 4x4 wheeled all-terrain vehicle made by Panhard. It comes in different versions. This vehicle was created to be as agile as the Peugeot P4 liaison car while providing protection against small weapons, artillery fragments, mines, and NBC weapons. It was produced from 1985 to 2010 and has been used by the French army and armies in Europe, Africa, and Central America in various conflicts since the 1980s.

Carlitto's Way is a 1993 American crime movie. Brian de Palma directed it. The story comes from novels by Judge Edwin Torres. David Koepp wrote the script. Al Pacino, Sean Penn, Penelope Ann Miller, Luis Guzmán, John Leguizamo, Jorge Porcel, Joseph Siravo, and Viggo Mortensen acted in it. Pacino plays Carlito Brigante, a Puerto Rican criminal who wants to stop being a criminal and live in paradise. But his past catches up with him, and he gets involved in criminal activities again. The movie is mostly based on "After Hours," but uses "Carlito's Way" as its title to avoid confusion with another movie. Critics had mixed opinions about the film, and it didn't do well at the box office. However, it later became a cult favorite. Penn and Miller were nominated for Golden Globes for their roles. A prequel based on the first novel came out in 2005.

neurosis refers to a type of mental issue causing ongoing worry, but without false beliefs or seeing things that aren't there. The term is not used by doctors anymore in the U.S., as it was removed from the "Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders" in 1980 with the release of the third edition. However, some people still use it. Neurosis is different from psychosis, which means losing contact with reality. It is also distinct from neuroticism, a key part of how people act and feel.

Samantha Anne Bee, born on October 25, 1969, is a comedian, writer, producer, political commentator, actress, and television host. She gained fame as a correspondent on "The Daily Show with Jon Stewart," where she was the longest-serving regular correspondent. In 2015, after 12 years, she left the show to start her own program, "Full Frontal with Samantha Bee." In 2014, Bee became a U.S. citizen but kept her Canadian citizenship. In 2017, she was named one of the 100 most influential people in the world by Time magazine.

Coriolanus is a tragedy by Shakespeare, likely written between 1605 and 1608. It's about the life of the Roman leader Caius Marcius Coriolanus. This play is one of Shakespeare's last two tragedies, along with "Antony and Cleopatra." Coriolanus was a Roman general known for his military success against uprisings. After this success, he tried to become a political leader. However, his personality didn't fit with the people, and he lost his position. Then, he made alliances to try to fix things his way. These alliances led to his downfall.

Anil Adhikari, born on May 30, 1987, and known as Yama Buddha, was a Nepalese rapper. He was one of the most famous rappers in Nepal. Some of his popular songs include "Sathi," "Aama," "Audai Chhu Ma," "Yo Prasanga," and "Antya Ko Suruwat." He created and hosted a popular rap battle show called "Raw Barz." He passed away on January 14, 2017.

Dirty paper coding, or DPC, is a method used in telecommunications to send digital data effectively through a channel with known interference. It works by adjusting the data before sending it to cancel out the interference. DPC allows for the maximum possible data transmission without extra power and without the receiver needing to know about the interference. The term "dirty paper coding" comes from an analogy. Imagine writing a message on a piece of paper that has random ink spots. By covering up and adding ink in the right places, you can still convey the same message as if the paper were clean, even though the reader doesn't know about the ink spots. In this analogy, the paper is the channel, the ink spots are the interference, the writer is the transmitter, and the reader is the receiver. At the transmitter, DPC is like reversing the process at the receiver in Wyner-Ziv coding.

An atlas is a group of maps. It usually shows maps of the Earth or a part of it. Atlases were traditionally kept in book form, but now they can be in digital or other multimedia formats. Besides showing places and borders, many atlases include data on politics, society, religion, and economics. They also provide information about the maps and the places shown.

Humayun Ahmed (born on November 13, 1948, and passed away on July 19, 2012) was a writer from Bangladesh. He wrote novels, plays, screenplays, and songs. He taught too. His first famous novel, "Nondito Noroke," came out in 1972. He wrote more than 200 books, and many were very popular in Bangladesh. His books were the best-selling at the Ekushey Book Fair in the 1990s and 2000s. He won important awards, like the Bangla Academy Literary Award in 1981 and the Ekushey Padak in 1994. In the early 1990s, he started making films based on his novels. He directed eight films and won six Bangladesh National Film Awards. He also had his own movie company called Nuhash Chalachitra.

defunctland is a YouTube show that keeps track of old amusement parks and rides. Created by Kevin Perjurer, it talks about the history and closure of theme parks and attractions worldwide, especially from Disney, Universal, and Six Flags. It started on February 15, 2017, and is well-regarded for its detailed research and good production quality. The channel has more than 700,000 subscribers. The success of defunctland led to two new shows: debunkedland and defuncttv, both launched in 2018.

Mexican Americans are people with full or partial Mexican ancestry in the United States. As of July 2018, they made up 11.3% of the U.S. population, with 37 million people claiming Mexican heritage. About 61.9% of all Latinos in the U.S. are Mexican Americans. Many live in the American Southwest, with over 60% in California and Texas. In 2016, Mexicans were 53% of foreign-born Latinos, and the U.S. had the second-largest Mexican community, after Mexico itself, comprising more than 24% of the world's Mexican-origin population. Mexican American families with indigenous roots have lived in the country for at least 15,000 years. The history of mestizo Mexican Americans dates back over 400 years, starting with the 1598 founding of Spanish New Mexico. The majority of historically Hispanic populations eventually switched to English. About 10% of current Mexican Americans are descendants of early colonial settlers who became U.S. citizens in 1848. Despite being officially considered white, many faced discrimination based on anti-Mexican sentiment and Hispanophobia. Indigenous Mexican Americans, like Pueblo, were granted citizenship in the 1920s. After the 1910 Mexican Revolution, continuous migration added to the population. During the Great Depression, Mexican Americans were scapegoated and subjected to mass deportations, affecting about 500,000 to two million people. The federal government allowed state and local governments to deport citizens without due process. About 85% of those deported were U.S. citizens, with 60% being born in the U.S. The remaining population became more politically active during the 1930s and 1940s, including the 1965 Delano grape strike led by Dolores Huerta and César Chávez, which formed the United Farm Workers. The Chicano movement sought civil rights reforms, inspired by the civil rights movement. Demands ranged from restoring land grants to improved education and voting rights, reflecting a growing awareness of collective history. The Chicano walkouts in the 1960s marked the movement's radical phase. Immigration from Mexico increased in the 1980s and 1990s, peaking in the mid-2000s. In 2008, "Yes We Can" (Spanish: "Sí, se puede") was adopted by Barack Obama's campaign, highlighting the growing importance of the Mexican American vote. The Great Recession led to a loss in Mexican American wealth, and immigration from Mexico decreased. The failure to enact immigration reform polarized handling of a diverse population as Mexican Americans spread beyond traditional centers. In 2015, the U.S. admitted 157,227 Mexican immigrants, and 1.31 million Mexicans were on the waiting list for legal entry as of November 2016.

Louis Philippe I was king of France from 1830 to 1848 and the last king of the country. He was known as Duke of Chartres. During the revolutionary wars, he led troops but later left France in 1793 after the government decided to execute King Louis XVI. His father, Duke of Orléans, was also executed. Louis Philippe spent 21 years in exile until the Bourbon restoration. In 1830, he became king after his cousin Charles X had to give up his throne during the July Revolution. His rule, called the July Monarchy, was supported by rich business people. He followed conservative policies, especially with help from French politician François Guizot. He also made friends with Britain and expanded France's colonies, including the conquest of Algeria. His popularity dropped in 1847 due to France's worsening economy. He lost his throne during the 1848 French Revolution and lived in exile in the United Kingdom. His followers were called Orléanists, while those supporting the main royal family were called Legitimists.

The Orient Express was a long-distance train created in 1883 by Compagnie Internationale des Wagons-Lits. The train's route and cars changed many times. In the past, different routes used the Orient Express name. The original Orient Express was just an international train service, but its name became known for mystery and luxury travel. Paris and Istanbul were the main cities the train went to, even though its planned route changed. The Orient Express was a symbol of luxury and comfort when travel was difficult. In 1977, the train stopped going to Istanbul. The next train, which only went to Budapest, ran for the last time on June 8, 2007. After that, the train started from Strasbourg instead because of faster travel times. The train left Strasbourg daily and joined another overnight train from Amsterdam. In 2009, the Orient Express stopped running completely. A private train called the Venice-Simplon Orient Express, which uses old cars from the 1920s and 1930s, still runs from London to Venice and other places in Europe. This includes the original Paris to Istanbul route.

The University of Houston (UH) is a public research university in Houston, Texas, and the main institution of the University of Houston system. Founded in 1927, UH has over 46,000 students. Its main campus covers 667 acres in southeast Houston. From 1983 to 1991, it was known as University of Houston–University Park. UH is a very big university with lots of research. It has more than 282 degree programs across 14 academic colleges, including programs for architecture, law, optometry, and pharmacy. The university does over $150 million in research each year and runs over 40 research centers and institutes. UH focuses on research in areas like superconductivity, space commercialization, biomedical sciences, energy, natural resources, and artificial intelligence. It awards more than 9,000 degrees each year, and its alumni base is over 260,000. The university's economic impact adds over $3 billion to the Texas economy annually and creates about 24,000 jobs. UH offers many performances, concerts, lectures, and events. It has over 400 student organizations and 17 intercollegiate sports teams. Annual events include Cat's Back, Homecoming, and Frontier Fiesta. The university’s athletic teams, known as the Houston Cougars, are part of the American Athletic Conference and play in the NCAA Division I. The football team often plays in bowl games, and the men's basketball team has made 21 NCAA tournament appearances, including five in the Final Four. The men's golf team has won 16 national championships, the most in NCAA history.

Ikaalinen is a town and municipality in Finland, part of the Pirkanmaa region. It has about 20,000 people and covers an area of 114 square kilometers, with 16 square kilometers of water. The population density is around 177 people per square kilometer. Neighboring municipalities are Hämeenkyrö, Jämijärvi, Kankaanpää, Parkano, Sastamala, and Ylöjärvi. Ikaalinen is a Finnish-speaking area. The Seitseminen National Park partly lies within it. Ikaalinen is an old tourist spot. Its spa history goes back a long time, and people love its beautiful landscape. In recent years, it has become a center for services, with good businesses, schools, and fun activities. Now, about 55% of people work in services, and 15% in farming, which is important for income. The most famous person from Ikaalinen is S. Albert Kivinen, a philosophy professor from the University of Helsinki. He is known for his humorous horror stories in a style like H.P. Lovecraft. His famous work, "Keskiyön mato Ikaalisissa" (The Midnight Worm in Ikaalinen), is about his childhood in Ikaalinen. Ikaalinen became a municipality in 1641. The market town was founded in 1858. In 1972, the market town and municipality merged, and Ikaalinen became a town in 1977. The town center is near Lake Kyrösjärvi, close to Highway 3 (E12). Major industries are Upofloor, Georgia Pacific Paper, E Avenue, and Katsa.

In 1972, the American Broadcasting Company (ABC) created the term "after-school special." These were usually TV movies that discussed important or controversial topics. They were shown in the late afternoon, often for school-age children, especially teenagers. These specials were shown 4 to 6 times a year, taking the place of local programming in the late afternoon. CBS had its own shows called "CBS Afternoon Playhouse," later known as "CBS Schoolbreak Special." They also had "Famous Classic Tales," which showed Australian cartoons based on literature. NBC had after-school programs called "Special Treat." ABC had its own "ABC After-school Special" and other similar programs like "ABC Saturday Superstar Movie" and "ABC Weekend Special."
Coyolles is a commune in Aisne, which is in Hauts-de-France, in northern France. Before the French Revolution, Coyolles was the center of the deanery of the Diocese of Soissons.

Bisma Karisma, born on November 27, 1990, in Bandung, is known for being a member of the boy band SM*SH. Before joining SM*SH, she was a national breakdancer and played the drums, percussion, and sang. With SM*SH, she has released two albums and won over forty awards. Their first album sold more than one million copies in six months and was awarded platinum. In mid-2014, Bisma started his solo career with the single "Lakukanlah." He wrote and composed the song himself. In 2016, Bisma was in a TV soap opera called Cinta Cenat Cenut. He also became a co-producer, wrote the original soundtrack, and was one of the main actors in the drama Juara.

"Troublemaker" is a song by British singer Olly Murs. It was released as the first single from his album "Right Place Right Time" in 2012. The song features American rapper Flo Rida. Murs, Flo Rida, Steve Robson, and Claude Kelly wrote the song. Steve Robson produced it. It first played on Capital FM radio on October 8, 2012, and was available to buy online on October 12, 2012, in some countries. The song was very successful. In the UK, it was the top single when it came out, making it Murs's fourth number-one solo single and his first to stay at the top for more than a week. The song also closed Murs's 2013 arena tour. As of November 2016, it was Murs's biggest-selling single.
Montord is a town in the Allier area of central France.

Mohammed Aamir Hussain Khan was born on March 14, 1965. He is an Indian actor, director, filmmaker, and host of TV talk shows. With a career spanning over thirty years, he is one of the most popular and influential actors in Indian cinema. He has a large following, especially in India and China. Newsweek calls him the biggest movie star in the world. Khan has won many awards, including nine Filmfare Awards, four National Film Awards, and an AACTA Award. He was honored by the Indian government with the Padma Shri in 2003 and the Padma Bhushan in 2010. In 2017, he received an honorary title from the Chinese government. He has been among the 500 most influential Muslims in the world for years. Khan started his acting career as a child actor in his uncle's film "Yaadon Ki Baaraat" in 1973. As an adult, his first important role was in the 1984 film "Holi." His first leading role was in "Qayamat Se Qayamat Tak" in 1988. His performance in this film and the thriller "Raakh" in 1989 earned him a National Film Award. In the 1990s, he became a leading actor in Hindi cinema with popular films like "Dil" (1990) and "Raja Hindustani" (1996), for which he won his first Filmfare Award for best actor. He also starred in "Sarfarosh" (1999). In 1999, he started his own production company, "Aamir Khan Productions." His first film, "Lagaan" (2001), was nominated for an Academy Award and won him more Filmfare Awards. After a four-year break, he returned with big hits like "Fanaa" (2006) and "Rang De Basanti" (2006). He directed his first film, "Taare Zameen Par" (2007), which was successful and earned him Filmfare Awards for best film and best director. His films often deal with social issues in India and mix entertainment with messages. Khan is also involved in social activism. He hosts a TV talk show called "Satyamev Jayate," which highlights social issues in India. His work on social issues, such as poverty, education, and discrimination, has earned him recognition. He was on the "Time" 100 list of influential people. Khan has been married twice. He was married to Reena Dutta for 15 years and then to film director Kiran Rao. He has three children, two from his first marriage and one from his second through surrogacy.

The corn snake, also known as "pantherophis guttatus," is a type of rat snake found in North America. It catches small animals by squeezing them. This snake is common in the southeastern and central parts of the United States. People often confuse it with the venomous copperhead snake and might accidentally kill it. However, corn snakes don't have venom and are safe for humans. They help control pests like mice and rats that damage crops and spread disease. Because they are calm, don't usually bite, are not too big, have a pretty pattern, and are easy to care for, they are often kept as pets. Corn snakes get their name from their frequent presence near places where corn is stored. They eat mice and rats that eat the corn. Some people say the name comes from how their belly scales look like the kernels of corn. Regardless of its origin, the name can help you recognize a corn snake.

"A Brief History of Time" is a book about the universe by physicist Stephen Hawking. First published in 1988, it explains complex ideas in simple terms for readers with no background knowledge of astronomy or physics. In the book, Hawking talks about the structure, origin, and future of the universe. He explains basic ideas like space and time, and the main forces that shape the universe, such as gravity. He also discusses important phenomena like the big bang and black holes. Hawking covers two major theories, general relativity and quantum mechanics, which scientists use to understand the universe. He explores the search for a single theory that can explain everything in the universe. The book became very popular and sold over 25 million copies.

Enzymes are proteins that speed up chemical reactions. They change substances called substrates into other molecules called products. Almost all processes in cells need enzymes to work quickly enough for life to continue. Enzymes help each step in metabolic pathways. The study of enzymes is called enzymology. A new field looks at enzymes that have lost their ability to catalyze reactions due to evolution. Enzymes can speed up more than 5,000 types of chemical reactions. RNA molecules, called ribozymes, can also act as catalysts. Enzymes work because of their unique shapes. Like other catalysts, enzymes don't change or use up in reactions. They just make reactions happen faster. Some enzymes can make reactions millions of times faster. An example is orotidine 5'-phosphate decarboxylase, which speeds up a reaction that would otherwise take millions of years to just milliseconds. Enzymes can be affected by other molecules. Some slow them down (inhibitors) and some speed them up (activators). Many medicines and poisons work by inhibiting enzymes. Enzyme activity changes outside their best working temperature and pH. Heat can destroy enzymes, making them lose their shape and ability to catalyze reactions. Some enzymes are used in factories to make antibiotics. Enzymes in laundry detergents break down stains, and in meat tenderizers, they help break down proteins, making the meat easier to eat.

Presidio Ahú was a prison in Curitiba, a city in Paraná, Brazil. It was the first prison in Curitiba and opened in 1905. The prison closed in 2006. Now, the site is used for filming movies and TV shows.
Rachel Mary Berkeley Portman, OBE, was born on December 11, 1960. She is an English composer famous for composing music for films.
I was a queen in Egypt during the fourth dynasty, around 2600 BC.

Dr. Lo Wing-lok, JP, was a doctor and politician from Hong Kong. He was a legislative councillor from 2000 to 2004, representing the medical functional constituency. In late 2007, he left the pro-democracy League of Social Democrats. He tried to become a legislative councillor again in 2004, 2008, and 2012 but was not successful. Dr. Lo died in 2015 from lung cancer.

Cumberland is a city in Cass County, Iowa, United States. It was founded in 1884. The population in 2010 was 262. Cumberland has a sister city called Massena, which is also in Iowa.

Michael P. Botticelli, born on January 2, 1958, is an American public health official. He worked as the director of the White House Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP) from March 2014 until the end of President Obama's term. He took the role after Gil Kerlikowske left. The U.S. Senate confirmed him in February 2015. Before his ONDCP job, he worked at the Massachusetts Department of Public Health. After finishing his ONDCP role, he became the executive director of the Grayken Center for Addiction Medicine at Boston Medical Center.

Paul the octopus lived from January 26, 2008, to October 26, 2010. He was a common octopus that predicted football match results. He became famous during the 2010 World Cup. His keepers put food in two boxes with different team flags. Paul would eat from the box with the flag of the winning team. He mostly predicted matches involving the German national team. Paul correctly guessed the winners in four out of six Euro 2008 matches and all seven matches in the 2010 World Cup, including Germany's win against Uruguay. He also correctly predicted Spain as the 2010 FIFA World Cup winner. Overall, Paul was right 12 times out of 14 predictions, with an 85.7% success rate.

Nordmann fir, also known as the Caucasian fir, is a tree that grows naturally in the mountains south and east of the Black Sea, in countries like Turkey, Georgia, and Russia's Caucasus region. It is found at elevations between 900 and 2,200 meters on mountains that receive more than 1,000 millimeters of rain. During the Ice Age, the current range of the Nordmann fir was connected to areas along the eastern and southern Black Sea coast. Despite the current climate being suitable, the tree does not grow in parts of the eastern Greater Caucasus that are more than 400 to 500 kilometers away from the Black Sea coast.
Randall Paul Stout was an architect based in Los Angeles, California. He lived from May 6, 1958, to July 11, 2014.

Lisbon is a small village in Claiborne Parish, Louisiana, United States. It had 185 people living there in 2010. Lisbon is east of the city of Homer, which is the parish seat. In the late 1800s, Lisbon had a school called the Lisbon Academy. T. H. Harris, who later became the state superintendent of education from 1908 to 1940, briefly attended this school. Another important person from Lisbon was John Sparks Patton. He was born there and later worked as a member of the Louisiana Public Service Commission from 1939 to 1944. Patton lost two races against T. H. Harris to become state superintendent. He is remembered for being the first person to suggest that school textbooks should be paid for by taxpayers.

Bad Moms is a 2016 American comedy film. Jon Lucas and Scott Moore directed and wrote it. The actors in the movie include Mila Kunis, Kristen Bell, Kathryn Hahn, Jay Hernandez, Annie Mumolo, Jada Pinkett Smith, and Christina Applegate. They started filming in New Orleans on January 11, 2016. The film had its premiere on July 19, 2016, in New York City and was shown in theaters on July 29, 2016, by STX Entertainment. Critics had mixed opinions about the movie, but it earned over $183 million worldwide. This was the first STX film to make over $100 million domestically. There was a sequel called "A Bad Moms Christmas" that came out on November 1, 2017.
Serres-Sainte-Marie is a commune in Pyrénées-Atlantiques, which is in southwestern France.

Respiratory diseases, or lung diseases, affect the organs and tissues that help air-breathing animals breathe. They can affect parts of the respiratory system, such as the trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, alveoli, pleura, and the muscles and nerves that control breathing. Some respiratory diseases, like a cold or flu, are mild and go away on their own. Others, like pneumonia or lung cancer, can be very serious and life-threatening. The study of these diseases is called pulmonology. Doctors who specialize in this field are called pulmonologists or respirologists. Respiratory diseases can be grouped in different ways, depending on which part of the respiratory system is affected, the symptoms shown, or what causes the disease.

Charles Quinton Murphy, born on July 12, 1959, and died on April 12, 2017, was an American actor, comedian, and writer. He was famous for writing and being part of the comedy show "Chappelle's Show" on Comedy Central. He also starred in the sitcom "Black Jesus." His older brother is comedian Eddie Murphy.

Hispar Pass (also known as Hispar La) is a high mountain pass in Pakistan, at an elevation of 5,128 meters (16,824 feet). It is in the Karakoram range. At this pass, two glaciers meet: the Biafo Glacier, which is 63 kilometers long, and the Hispar Glacier, which is 49 kilometers long. Together, they form a long ice path that is 100 kilometers in length, the longest such path outside of the polar regions.
Gurdon is a city in Clark County, Arkansas, United States. The population was 2,212 in 2010.

Brighton is a village in Macoupin County, Illinois, and part of Jersey County. According to the 2010 U.S. Census, Brighton had 2,254 people living there. The current mayor is Michael Roberts. Brighton is in the Metro-East region and the St. Louis area.

Miguel Kaku, born on January 24, 1947, is an American physicist who also talks about science and writes about it. He teaches physics at the City College of New York and the CUNY Graduate Center. Kaku has written several popular books, including "Physics of the Impossible" (2008), "Physics of the Future" (2011), and "The Future of the Mind" (2014). He often appears on TV and radio, writes online, and has hosted specials for the BBC, Discovery Channel, History Channel, and Science Channel.

Manuel Luis Quezon y Molina (August 19, 1878 – August 1, 1944), known as MLQ, was a Filipino leader who was the first president of the entire Philippines from 1935 to 1944. During his presidency, he helped peasants and improved the military, among other things. He established a government in the United States when Japan invaded. Quezon died of tuberculosis in New York and was buried in Arlington National Cemetery. After the war, his remains were moved to Manila, and he is buried at the Quezon Memorial Circle. Quezon was given a special medal in 2015 by the International Raoul Wallenberg Foundation for helping people during the Holocaust between 1937 and 1941. This recognition was shared with the people of the Philippines.

The chloralkali process is used to make chlorine and sodium hydroxide (lye/caustic soda) by electrolyzing sodium chloride solutions. This process began on a large scale in 1892. In this process, brine (saltwater) is used to produce sodium hydroxide, hydrogen, and chlorine. Using calcium chloride or potassium chloride instead of sodium chloride results in different products. The process uses a lot of electricity—about 2500 kWh per ton of sodium hydroxide. Chlorine and sodium hydroxide are produced in equal amounts, so they need to be used together. For every mole of chlorine produced, one mole of hydrogen is also produced. Much of the hydrogen is used to make hydrochloric acid, ammonia, hydrogen peroxide, or for producing power and steam.

James P. Molinaro, born on March 11, 1931, is an American politician. He used to be the borough president of Staten Island. Molinaro won his first election as borough president on November 6, 2001, defeating his opponent, Jerome X. O'Donovan, by 50% to 43%. He started his term on January 1, 2002. Molinaro was re-elected for a third term on November 3, 2009, with 46,061 votes (62.7%). His opponent, John Luisi, got 27,356 votes (37.3%). Luisi also challenged Molinaro in 2005.

Guangdong, also called Canton Province, is a coastal province in southern China near the South China Sea. Its capital is Guangzhou. As of 2018, it had 113.46 million people, making it the most populous province in China. The province is the 15th largest by area. Guangdong's economy is very big, with a GDP of $1.47 trillion in 2018, ranking fourth globally. A key area is the Pearl River Delta, known for high-tech, manufacturing, and trade. Guangzhou and Shenzhen, two important cities here, are among the most populous and influential in China. Guangdong surpassed Henan and Shandong to become China's most populous province in 2005. It now has over 108 million people. Most of historical Guangdong is now part of the People's Republic of China, except for some islands controlled by Taiwan. Guangdong's economy has grown since then. Since 1989, it has been the top in total GDP among all Chinese provinces. It borders Hong Kong to the south, which has helped its economy. Guangdong is also known for spreading its culture, including languages, music, food, and traditions, throughout China, Southeast Asia, and other countries. This cultural influence extends to Hong Kong and Macau, as well as Chinese communities in Singapore and Malaysia.

The Tagalog Wikipedia is the Tagalog version of Wikipedia. It started on December 1, 2003. As of now, it has fewer articles. The Cebuano Wikipedia has more articles, with over 30,000. The Waray Wikipedia also has many articles, over 20,000. Most of the articles in Cebuano and Waray were made by a bot called LSJbot. However, the Tagalog Wikipedia has more active users. It has around 1,500 active users. The Cebuano Wikipedia has about 600 active users, and the Waray Wikipedia has around 300 active users.

In math, the intermediate value theorem says: If a function ``f'' is continuous and its domain includes the interval [``a'', ``b''], then it will take on any value between ``f''(``a'') and ``f''(``b'') at some point within that interval. This idea has two key results.
Günther Maleuda was an East German politician. He lived from January 20, 1931, to July 18, 2012. From 1989 to 1990, he was the president of the People's Chamber, which was the East German parliament.
Saint-Samson is a commune in Calvados, which is in the Normandy region of northwestern France.

The British Rail class 22, also called "baby warship," were diesel-hydraulic locomotives made for the western region of British Railways. They looked like the class 21 diesel-electric locomotives. The name "baby warship" came from how they looked like and had similar equipment to the British Rail class D20/2 or class 41 "warship class." These locomotives had numbers from D6300 to D6357.

Stara Zagora is a province in central Bulgaria. It was previously called Stara Zagora okrug. The province has its name from the city of Stara Zagora, which is the sixth-largest town in the country. Stara Zagora is also the main city in the province. The province includes 11 municipalities and had 350,925 people as of December 2009. In the southeast part of the province, near the Radnevo municipality, there is a coal mine. Between 1934 and 1949, Stara Zagora province also covered some areas of today's Kardzhali province.
Covid-19 was found in Rwanda in March 2020.

The Kinsey reports are two books about human sexuality: "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male" (1948) and "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female" (1953). Alfred Kinsey wrote these books with help from Wardell Pomeroy, Clyde Martin, and Paul Gebhard. The books were very popular but also caused controversy among scientists and the general public. They challenged common beliefs and discussed topics that were not usually talked about. Some people questioned Kinsey's methods. Kinsey was a scientist at Indiana University who started the Kinsey Institute for researching sex, gender, and reproduction. He collected data for "Sexual Behavior in the Human Male" from about 5,300 men over 15 years. For "Sexual Behavior in the Human Female," he interviewed around 6,000 women. His book looked at how often women engage in different sexual activities and how things like age, money, and religion affect their behavior. He compared women's and men's sexual activities. Kinsey's evidence suggested women are less sexually active than men. Some criticized Kinsey's method of collecting data. There were concerns that some information might have come from people who had done bad things to children. The Kinsey Institute said this wasn't true but acknowledged that men who had had sexual experiences with children were interviewed. They said Kinsey made sure these people's identities stayed private to get honest answers, and the chance of their crimes continuing was low. Later, researchers thought Kinsey might have overestimated same-sex attraction because of how he chose people to talk to. However, his work is still seen as very important and one of the best-known studies on sex.

Ellen Louise Axson Wilson (born Axson; May 15, 1860 – August 6, 1914) was Woodrow Wilson's first wife and the mother of their three daughters. She was from the South and came from a family of ministers. She was born in Savannah, Georgia, but grew up in Rome, Georgia. She liked art and studied at the Art Students League of New York before marrying Woodrow Wilson. She continued to make art later in life. She was the First Lady from 1913 until her death in 1914. During this time, she helped arrange weddings for two of their daughters in the White House.

Hudson Hawk is a 1991 American action comedy film directed by Michael Lehmann. Bruce Willis stars as the main character and also helped write the story and the theme song. Danny Aiello, Andie MacDowell, James Coburn, David Caruso, Lorraine Toussaint, Frank Stallone, Sandra Bernhard, and Richard E. Grant also appear in the movie. The film uses cartoon-style jokes with lots of sound effects, adding to its silly humor. The story mixes ideas from conspiracy theories, secret groups, and old mysteries, along with funny inventions. Hudson and his partner Tommy "Five-Tone" (played by Danny Aiello) often sing songs at the same time to stay in sync during their adventures. Willis and Aiello perform duets of "Swinging on a Star" by Bing Crosby and "Side by Side" by Paul Anka in the movie. The film wasn't popular in the U.S., earning only $17 million, and received three Razzies, including the worst picture award. However, it did better overseas, making $80 million, for a total of $97 million worldwide.
Sargodha division is a part of Punjab province in Pakistan. The capital city is Sargodha. In 2017, the division had about 8.18 million people.

Pierre Steffen Baigorry, known as Peter Fox, was born on September 3, 1971. He is a German singer, songwriter, musician, and music video director. Peter Fox is also a member of the German reggae and dancehall band Seeed.

"Island of the Blue Dolphins" is a 1960 book for children written by Scott O'Dell. The story is about a 12-year-old girl named Karana who spends years alone on an island off the California coast. The story is based on the real-life story of Juana Maria, a Native American who was left alone for 18 years on San Nicolas Island in the 19th century. The book won the Newbery Medal in 1961. It was made into a movie in 1964. O'Dell wrote a sequel called "Zia," which came out in 1976. The 50th anniversary edition of "Island of the Blue Dolphins" has a new introduction by Lois Lowry, a writer who won the Newbery Medal. It also includes parts of a book about burials from Father Gonzales Rubio of the Santa Barbara Mission. In 2016, a new edition of "Island of the Blue Dolphins" was published. This edition includes chapters that were removed before the book was first published.
Ahmed Salah Mohamed Hosni Hassan, born on July 11, 1979, was an Egyptian footballer. He played as a striker and is now retired.

Torii Hunter was born on July 18, 1975. He played professional baseball as a center fielder and right fielder. He played for the Minnesota Twins, Los Angeles Angels of Anaheim, and Detroit Tigers from 1997 to 2015. Hunter was an all-star five times and won nine consecutive Gold Glove awards as a center fielder. He also won the Silver Slugger award twice.

St Michael's Cathedral, also known as Coventry Cathedral, is the main church of the Bishop of Coventry and the Diocese of Coventry in the Church of England. It is in Coventry, West Midlands, England. The current bishop is Christopher Cocksworth and the current dean is John Witcombe. The city of Coventry has had three cathedrals. The first one was St Mary's, a monastic building. Only some ruins of it are left. The second was St Michael's, a 14th-century Gothic church. It became a cathedral later but was destroyed during World War II, leaving only a ruined shell. The third is the new St Michael's Cathedral, built after the old one was destroyed.

The National Assembly of Thailand (abbreviated as NAT) is the legislative branch with two chambers in the Thai government. It meets at Sappaya-Sapasathan in the Dusit district of Bangkok. The National Assembly was created in 1932 when Thailand adopted its first constitution, changing the country from an absolute monarchy to a constitutional monarchy. During the 2013 political crisis, the House of Representatives was dissolved by Prime Minister Yingluck Shinawatra. She called for an election on February 2, 2014, but this was later canceled by the Constitutional Court. After the 2014 military coup, the National Assembly was replaced by the National Legislative Assembly, a single-chamber body supported by the military, based on the 2014 constitution. When the 2017 constitution was officially adopted in April 2017, the National Assembly was recreated. However, the National Legislative Assembly, supported by the military, could continue to exist until the new National Assembly was formed after the 2019 general election.

Vijaya Mulay was born on May 16, 1921, and died on May 19, 2019. She was a filmmaker, historian, writer, educator, and researcher. Her close friendships with directors Satyajit Ray, Louis Malle, and Mrinal Sen, among others, gave her special insights into Indian cinema that influenced her work. Her work has helped others understand India better. She is the mother of Suhasini Mulay, a national award-winning actor, and her son-in-law is Atul Gurtu, a high-energy physicist. Vijaya Mulay is known for her animated film "Ek Anek Aur Ekta," which won the National Film Award for the best educational film.

Ivan Hašek, born on September 6, 1963, was a Czech football player. He played as a central midfielder. He spent 11 years with Sparta Prague, playing in over 300 official games. Later, he managed the team. Hašek also played for Czechoslovakia in the 1990 World Cup. He was also the president of the Czech Republic's football association.
Billy used to be a commune in Calvados, which is in Normandy, a region in northwestern France. On January 1, 2017, Billy became part of a new commune called Valambray.
Glos is a commune in Calvados, which is in the Normandy region of northwestern France.
Egliswil is a village and municipality in the district of Lenzburg, in the canton of Aargau, Switzerland.

The Katiti Aboriginal Land Trust (Katiti ALT) is a land trust in the southwest of the Northern Territory, Australia. It was created in 1980 through the Katiti Land Claim. The trust includes Pitjantjatjara, Yankunytjatjara, and Luritja people. The land is officially known as Northern Territory portion 1818. It borders Petermann Land Trust and Uluṟu–Kata Tjuṯa National Park to the north and west. To the east and south are two pastoral stations, Curtin Springs and Mulga Park. The town of Yulara is not part of the land trust and is between the Katiti block and Uluṟu–Kata Tjuṯa National Park. Katiti ALT is named after Katiti, a natural spring located south of Lake Amadeus. Baldwin Spencer and Francis James Gillen first wrote about this spring in 1894. They called it "Kurtitina." Lawrence Wells' prospecting expedition visited it in 1903, and Herbert Basedow later marked it on his maps as "Curtyteena."

Kansas is now divided into 4 congressional districts. Each district has a representative in the United States House of Representatives. The number of districts didn't change after the 2010 census. From 2010 to 2018, all representatives from Kansas were Republicans. In 2018, a Democratic candidate won a seat, making the delegation 3 Republicans and 1 Democrat.

The Institute for Research on Public Policy (IRPP) is an independent, bilingual, not-for-profit organization in Montreal, Quebec. Its goal is to improve public policy in Canada by creating research, offering insights, and helping discussions about current and future policy issues for Canadians and their governments. IRPP publishes research and organizes events like conferences, round tables, and panel discussions for stakeholders, academics, policymakers, and the public. They also publish a magazine called "Policy Options." IRPP focuses on four main issues: how Canada's communities are changing, meeting Canada's innovation challenges, income inequality, and the impact of global trade on the Canadian economy. The IRPP was created in 1968 by then Prime Minister Pierre Elliott Trudeau's commitment to establish an independent institute for public policy research. The government and private sector funded an endowment for the institute in the early 1970s. The IRPP is a registered charity and is incorporated under Canadian law. Anne McLeod is the current board chair, and Graham Fox is the current president and CEO.

Air Dolomiti S.p.A. is an Italian regional airline based in Dossobuono, Villafranca di Verona, Italy. It has operating bases at Munich Airport and Frankfurt Airport in Germany. Air Dolomiti is completely owned by Lufthansa. The airline flies to and from Munich and Frankfurt from several Italian cities. Most of the flights are sold under the Air Dolomiti brand and are also operated by Lufthansa. A few flights remain under the Lufthansa brand.
Davids Wayne, born Wayne James McMeekan on January 30, 1914, died on February 9, 1995. He was an American actor who performed on stage and in movies. His career lasted for more than 50 years.
Janine Sutto was born in France in 1921 and died in 2017. She was a Canadian actress and comedian.

Antonino Rocca, born Antonino Biasetton, was born on April 13, 1921, and died on March 15, 1977. He was an Italian professional wrestler who worked in Argentina. Antonino teamed up with Miguel Pérez as a tag team. After he died, he was honored and inducted into the WWF Hall of Fame in 1995. He was also included in the Wrestling Observer Newsletter Hall of Fame in 1996.

Slim Harpo, born James Isaac Moore on January 11, 1924, and died on January 31, 1970, was a famous American blues musician. He was known for playing swamp blues and was very successful, one of the top blues artists of his time. Some of his most popular songs were "I'm a King Bee" in 1957, "Rainin' in My Heart" in 1961, and "Baby Scratch My Back" in 1966. These songs did well, reaching number one on the R&B chart and number sixteen on the US pop chart. Slim Harpo's stage name came from the nickname for the blues harmonica, which is called the "harp."

The Celtic League is a group that promotes Celtic identity and culture. It was created in 1961. The group focuses on Ireland, Scotland, Wales, Brittany, Cornwall, and the Isle of Man, known as the Celtic nations. It especially wants to support the Celtic languages in these areas. The league also wants more self-governance for the Celtic nations and aims for each to become an independent country. The Celtic League is recognized by the United Nations for its work.

Lake Amadeus is a big salt lake in the southwest corner of the Northern Territory in Australia. It is about north of Uluru, also known as Ayers Rock. Nearby, there is a smaller lake called Lake Neale to the northwest. Lake Amadeus is part of the Amadeus Basin, which contains materials from the Petermann orogeny.

Ángela María Ponce Camacho is a Spanish model and beauty pageant winner. She won Miss Universe Spain in 2018. On June 29, 2018, she made history by becoming the first openly transgender woman to win Miss Spain. Ponce represented Spain in Miss Universe 2018 as the first openly transgender contestant. However, she did not advance to the finals.
