Blanco County is in Texas. It's part of the Edwards Plateau. In 2010, it had 10, 497 people. The county seat is Johnson City. Blanco County is named after the Blanco River, which goes through the county. Texas created Blanco County in 1858 from parts of Burnet, Comal, Gillespie, and Hays counties. Blanco was the county seat from 1858 to 1890. Then, the county seat moved to Johnson City.
Peoria County is in Illinois, a state in the U.S. The 2010 census showed it had 186, 494 people. Peoria is the county seat. Peoria County is part of the Peoria, IL metropolitan area.

Belkin International, Inc., is an American company that makes consumer electronics, especially connectivity devices. It is based in Playa Vista, Los Angeles, California. The company sells many types of products, such as routers, iPod and iPhone accessories, mobile computing accessories, surge protectors, network switches, hubs, USB and computer network cables, KVM switches, racks, enclosures, and other accessories. Belkin International owns the brands Belkin, Linksys, and Wemo, as well as a smart home water management company called Phyn.

Irrigation means applying water to plants at the right times. It helps grow crops, keep gardens healthy, and plant new areas during dry weather. Irrigation can also protect crops from frost, control weeds, and prevent soil from becoming compact. Without rain, farming that depends only on rainfall is called rain-fed. Irrigation systems are used for more than just farming. They can cool animals, reduce dust, treat sewage, and help in mining. Irrigation is often studied with drainage, which is removing extra water. People have been using irrigation for over 5,000 years in many places around the world, such as Asia and the southwestern United States.

x-Men: The Last Stand, also called x3 or x-Men 3, is a 2006 movie about superheroes. It follows the x-Men team from Marvel Comics. This is the third movie in the x-Men series, after x2 in 2003. Brett Ratner directed it, and Simon Kinberg and Zak Penn wrote it. The main actors include Hugh Jackman, Halle Berry, Ian McKellen, Famke Janssen, Anna Paquin, Kelsey Grammer, James Marsden, Rebecca Romijn, Shawn Ashmore, Aaron Stanford, Vinnie Jones, and Patrick Stewart. The movie is based on two comic book stories: "The Dark Phoenix Saga" and "Gifted." It tells the story of a cure for mutants that causes problems, and of Jean Grey coming back to life. Bryan Singer, who directed the first two x-Men movies, left to make Superman Returns. John Ottman and Dan Harris, Michael Dougherty, and James Marsden also left for the same reason. Filming took place from August 2005 to January 2006, with a budget of $210 million, making it the most expensive movie at the time. The movie came out on May 26, 2006, and earned about $459 million worldwide, making it the seventh-highest-grossing film of 2006 and the highest-grossing x-Men movie. Critics had mixed opinions, praising the acting, music, and action scenes but criticizing the script, overuse of characters, style, and lack of dynamics.

Rudi van Dantzig was born on August 4, 1933, and passed away on January 19, 2012. He was a Dutch choreographer, company director, and writer. Rudi van Dantzig played a crucial role in making Dutch ballet famous around the world in the latter part of the 20th century.

Parma is a city in northern Italy, part of the Emilia-Romagna region. It is known for its architecture, music, art, prosciutto (ham), cheese, and beautiful countryside. Parma has a university that is one of the oldest in the world. The city is split into two parts by a river. The area on the other side of the river is called "oltretorrente." The ancient Etruscans named the city after their round shield, which the Romans also used. A famous Italian poet, Attilio Bertolucci, once said that Parma needed a river as a big capital city, but as a small capital, it got a stream that is often dry.

A bottle cap or top seals the bottle's opening. It is usually decorated with the brand logo and comes in colors. For plastic bottles, plastic caps are used. For glass bottles, metal caps with a plastic backing are used; the metal is usually steel. Some plastic caps have a pour spout. Flip-top caps provide controlled dispensing of dry products. Often, the caps for plastic bottles are made of a different type of plastic than the bottle itself.

David Wark Griffith, born on January 22, 1875, and died on July 23, 1948, was an American film director. He is widely seen as the most important filmmaker of his time. He started making long movies, something new at the time. His movie "The Birth of a Nation" from 1915 made money for investors but also caused a lot of trouble because it showed African Americans in a bad way and made the Ku Klux Klan look good. To answer his critics, he made "Intolerance" in 1916, but it wasn't meant to say sorry for the bad images of African Americans. Some of Griffith's later movies, like "Broken Blossoms" in 1919, "Way Down East" in 1920, and "Orphans of the Storm" in 1921, were successful. However, he often spent too much money making and promoting his films, which led to them not doing well at the box office. By the time he made his last full-length movie, "The Struggle" in 1931, he had directed about 500 films. Together with Charlie Chaplin, Mary Pickford, and Douglas Fairbanks, Griffith helped start United Artists. This company let them control their own work instead of working with big movie studios. Griffith was also one of the people who started the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences.

A mathematical proof is an argument that shows a statement is true based on logical reasoning. It uses other established statements, like theorems, but can be built from basic assumptions called axioms and rules of logic. Proofs are like showing something is true for all cases, not just many. An unproven but believed statement is called a conjecture or a hypothesis. Proofs use symbols and natural language, but formal proofs, using only symbols, are in proof theory. Differences between formal and informal proofs have led to studies on mathematical practices and the philosophy of mathematics.

France has 44 world heritage sites recognized by UNESCO. These sites include 39 cultural properties, 4 natural properties, and 1 mixed property. Three of these sites are shared between countries. The first site was added in 1979, and the most recent was added in 2019. In 1979, five properties were submitted. France's tentative list includes 37 sites. UNESCO uses six cultural criteria (I, II, III, IV, V, VI) and four natural criteria (VII, VIII, IX, X) for selection. The dates on the world heritage list are the dates when the sites were added, while the tentative list dates show when they were first suggested. Each site has a unique number that links to its description on UNESCO's website.

Kimble County is in Texas. It's on the Edwards Plateau. In 2010, there were 4,607 people living there. The county seat is Junction. Kimble County was made in 1858 and officially started in 1876. It's named after George C. Kimble, who died at the Battle of the Alamo.
Gagny is a town in the eastern suburbs of Paris, France. It is situated close to the center of Paris.

The Salt Fork of the Arkansas River is a stream that joins the Arkansas River. It is located in southern Kansas and northern Oklahoma, in the United States. Through the Arkansas River, it is part of the Mississippi River watershed.

Elizabeth Bonnin was born on September 16, 1975. She is from France but lives in Ireland. She works as a science, wildlife, and nature TV presenter in both Ireland and the United Kingdom. She also studies and works in biology. In the early 2000s, she hosted morning and music shows. She is famous for presenting shows like "Galapagos," "How the Earth Works," "Animals in Love," "Stargazing Live," "Blue Planet Live," "Cats vs Dogs: Which is Best?" and "Should We Close Our Zoos?" From 2009 to 2014, she co-hosted the BBC series "Bang Goes the Theory." Since 2013, she has co-hosted "Countrywise" for ITV. In 2019, she presented "Meat: A Threat to Our Planet?"

Dominic Felix Amici, born on May 31, 1908, and passed away on December 6, 1993, was an American actor and comedian. He started his career by performing in college shows, stock productions, and vaudeville. In the early 1930s, he became a major radio star, leading to a movie contract with 20th Century Fox in 1935. As a handsome and charming leading man, he starred in 40 films over the next 14 years, appearing in comedies, dramas, and musicals. In the 1950s, he worked on Broadway and in television, hosting NBC's "International Showtime" from 1961 to 1965. Later in his career, he returned to film work and had a successful revival, playing a villain in "Trading Places" in 1983. For his performance in "Cocoon" in 1985, he won the Academy Award for best supporting actor.

Didier Yves Drogba, born on March 11, 1978, was a retired professional footballer who played as a striker. He is the all-time top scorer and former captain of the Ivory Coast national team. He is best known for his career at Chelsea, where he scored more goals than any other foreign player and is the club's fourth highest goal scorer of all time. Widely regarded as one of Chelsea's greatest players, Drogba was named in the Chelsea team of the 2010-2020 decade by Chelsea's fans. He was named African Footballer of the Year twice, in 2006 and 2009. Drogba started his professional career at Le Mans in the Ligue 2 when he was 18 years old. He signed his first professional contract at 21. In the 2002-2003 season, he scored 17 goals in 34 appearances for Guingamp in Ligue 1. He then moved to Olympique de Marseille, where he finished as the third highest scorer in the 2003-2004 season with 19 goals, helping the club reach the 2004 UEFA Cup final. In July 2004, Drogba moved to Chelsea for £24 million, making him the most expensive Ivorian player in history. In his debut season, he helped Chelsea win their first league title in 50 years. A year later, he won another Premier League title. His performances earned him a spot in the FIFA World XI for 2007. In March 2012, he became the first African player to score 100 Premier League goals. Two months later, he scored in Chelsea's 2012 FA Cup final win over Liverpool, becoming the first (and only) player to score in four separate FA Cup finals. He also played in the 2012 UEFA Champions League final, scoring the 88th-minute equaliser and the winning penalty in the deciding shootout against Bayern Munich. After playing in China and Turkey, Drogba returned to Chelsea in July 2014. He scored 10 goals in 10 finals and won 10 trophies, earning the title "ultimate big game player." In 2015, he joined Montreal Impact in Canada as a designated player, scoring 23 goals in 41 matches over two seasons. Drogba became a player-owner for Phoenix Rising of the United Soccer League in 2017 and retired a year later at 40. He was an Ivory Coast international from 2002 to 2014, captaining the national team from 2006 until his retirement. He is the nation's all-time top goalscorer with 65 goals from 105 appearances. He led Ivory Coast to their first FIFA World Cup appearance in 2006 and captained the team in the 2010 and 2014 FIFA World Cups. He retired from international football in 2014 and from professional football in 2018. In December 2018, he became vice president of the International Organization for Peace and Sport.

Rod Robert "Rod" Roddy (September 28, 1937 – October 27, 2003) was an American radio and TV announcer. He was famous for being an offstage announcer on game shows. He announced shows like "Whew!" and "Press Your Luck" on CBS. Roddy said "Come on down!" on "The Price is Right," even though Johnny Olson started using that phrase first. Roddy took over from Johnny Olson as the announcer for "The Price is Right" in 1986 and kept the job until he died in 2003. As of 2020, he was the longest-serving announcer on the show. Roddy also appeared on camera in some episodes of "Press Your Luck" and "The Price is Right." He was the voice of Mike the Microphone in "Disney's House of Mouse" from 2001 until his death.

Travers was a town in the Val-de-Travers district of the Neuchâtel canton in Switzerland. On January 1, 2009, Travers and several other towns—Boveresse, Buttes, Couvet, Fleurier, Les Bayards, Môtiers, Noiraigue, and Saint-Sulpice—merged to form Val-de-Travers.

Hurricane Dora was the first hurricane on record to hit the Florida coast. It was the sixth tropical storm and the second hurricane of the 1964 season. Dora formed from a tropical wave near Senegal on August 28. By September 3, it had become a Category 1 hurricane, reaching Category 2 intensity six hours later. On September 5, it strengthened to a Category 3, and later peaked as a Category 4 with winds of 130 mph. At 18:00 UTC on September 6, Dora weakened to a Category 3 hurricane and then to a Category 2 while moving westward. Approaching Florida's east coast on September 7, Dora maintained Category 2 intensity and made landfall near St. Augustine at 110 mph. By September 11, it had weakened to a tropical storm. Dora then moved over southwestern Georgia, before turning east-northeastward the next day and re-entering the Atlantic near Cape Hatteras, North Carolina. The remnants dissipated over Newfoundland on September 16. Along the coast, high tides and strong winds hit north Florida. In St. Augustine, sustained winds reached 125 mph. In Jacksonville, about 156,000 customers lost power, and 19% of phones in Duval County were out of service. Damage was mostly to older buildings and coastal areas. Flooding occurred near the St. Johns River. Heavy rain damaged crops and roads, isolating some communities for days. In Florida, 74 dwellings were destroyed, 9,374 received damage, 14 mobile homes were obliterated, and 218 others suffered severe damage. About 50 farm buildings and 423 small businesses were severely damaged or demolished. Three deaths and $230 million in damage occurred. In Georgia, about 1,135 homes were damaged, five were destroyed, 18 trailers suffered major impact, and 43 small businesses were damaged or destroyed. One death and $9 million in damage occurred. Dora caused $280 million in damage and five deaths in total.
An icon is a religious painting in the Christian tradition, coming from the Greek word meaning image. An icon can also refer to:

Samsung Galaxy S6 is a type of smartphone. It was made, released, and marketed by Samsung Electronics. It came after the Galaxy S5. There were actually two versions: Galaxy S6 and Galaxy S6 Edge. The Edge version had a screen that curved around the sides. Galaxy S6 and Edge were shown to the public on March 1, 2015, at a Samsung event in Barcelona. They were released on April 10, 2015. In August 2015, Samsung introduced a third model, the Galaxy S6 Edge+, which had a bigger screen, more memory, but no remote control feature. The S6's design was mostly metal with glass on the back, unlike the plastic of earlier models. It had a better camera, improved software, and could charge wirelessly. It also supported mobile payments. Critics mostly liked the S6, praising its quality and improved features. However, removing the ability to expand storage or remove the battery was seen as a negative. The S6 Edge was criticized for not making good use of its curved screen. The S7 replaced it in March 2016.

John Elliot was born on May 6, 1898, and died on September 18, 1988. He was a British transport and railway manager. His full name was John Elliot Blumenfeld. His father, R. D. Blumenfeld, was the editor of the "Daily Mail." Later, he became the managing editor of the "Daily Express." John changed his last name to Elliot in March 1923, as advised by Lord Beaverbrook.

Irredentism refers to movements that claim and try to take back territory, often based on historical or legendary reasons. People involved in these movements consider the land to be part of their nation. Sometimes, there are debates about the exact borders of these nations, which can lead to disagreements.

The KGB, or Committee for State Security, was the main security agency of the Soviet Union from 1954 until the country dissolved in 1991. It took over from earlier agencies like the Cheka, NKGB, NKVD, and MGB. The KGB reported to the Council of Ministers and was responsible for internal security, intelligence, and secret police work. Similar agencies operated in most Soviet republics, except for the Russian SFSR, and had many related ministries and committees. The KGB was a military service, governed by army laws, like the Soviet army or MVD internal troops. Most KGB archives are still secret, but two online sources exist. The main KGB functions included foreign intelligence, counter-intelligence, surveillance, guarding the USSR's borders, protecting the Communist Party leadership, securing government communications, and stopping nationalism, dissent, and anti-Soviet activities. In 1991, after the Soviet Union ended, the KGB split into the Federal Security Service and the Foreign Intelligence Service of the Russian Federation. In the early 1990s, with Russian help, South Ossetia, which had broken away from Georgia, set up its own KGB. Belarus also created its own security agency called the State Security Committee.
Tagsdorf is a commune in Haut-Rhin, which is in Alsace, in northeastern France.
Brienzwiler is a town in the Interlaken-Oberhasli area. It is part of the Bern canton in Switzerland. Besides Brienzwiler village, the town also includes Balmhof.

Parker Brothers was an American company that made toys and games. In 1991, it became part of Hasbro. Since 1883, they published over 1,800 games. Some of their popular games include Monopoly, Clue (called Cluedo in Britain), Sorry!, Risk, Trivial Pursuit, Ouija, Aggravation, Bop It, and Probe. After Parker Brothers closed, their games were marketed under the Hasbro Gaming label. However, in 2017, Hasbro brought back the Parker Brothers brand with new games that are similar to some of their well-known earlier games.
In seismology, the epicenter is the point on the ground directly above where an earthquake starts. This point is below the surface, called the hypocenter or focus.

Elephant polo is a type of polo played on elephants. It is played in Nepal, Rajasthan (India), and Thailand. Teams from England and Scotland also participate. The game uses a regular polo ball and sticks made of cane, similar to bamboo. The playing field is shorter than a normal polo field because elephants move slower. Two people ride each elephant. One person controls the elephant, and the other plays the game by telling the first person where to go and hitting the ball. The sport began in Meghauli, Nepal, and the headquarters is at Tiger Tops in Nepal. The World Elephant Polo Association organizes the world championships there. In Nepal and Thailand, the game follows rules set by the World Elephant Polo Association to protect the elephants. Other places, like India and Sri Lanka, run their own events. In Sri Lanka, an annual tournament was held in Galle. In 2007, an elephant caused trouble during a game, hurting players and damaging a team bus. Some people say elephant polo is cruel. This led to matches being canceled, sponsors leaving, and elephant polo being removed from Guinness World Records. In October 2018, Thailand decided to stop elephant polo matches.
Stapleton may refer to: A place A person's name

Lily Chloe Ninette Thomson, born on April 5, 1989, is known professionally as Lily James and is an English actress. She studied acting at the Guildhall School of Music and Drama in London. She began her acting career in a British TV series called "Just William" in 2010. After appearing in the period drama series "Downton Abbey" from 2012 to 2015, she became famous for playing Cinderella in the 2015 fantasy film. James then starred in "War & Peace" as Natasha Rostova in 2016. She appeared in several films, including "Baby Driver" (2017), "Darkest Hour" (2017), "The Guernsey Literary and Potato Peel Pie Society" (2018), "Mamma Mia! Here We Go Again" (2018), and "Yesterday" (2019).

Barley (hordeum vulgare) is a type of cereal grain in the grass family. It is grown in many parts of the world in cooler areas. Barley was one of the first grains people started growing, especially in Eurasia about 10,000 years ago. People use barley to feed animals, make beer and other alcoholic drinks, and as a healthy food. It is also used in soups and bread in different cultures. Barley grains can be turned into malt using an old method. In 2017, barley was the fourth most produced grain, after maize, rice, and wheat.

Gauss's law for magnetism is part of four main equations that describe classical electrodynamics. This law says that magnetic fields have no sources or sinks, meaning they are always enclosed in loops. In other words, magnetic monopoles, or single north or south magnetic poles, do not exist. Basic units of magnetism are magnetic dipoles, which have both north and south poles. If magnetic monopoles were discovered, this law would need to change. Gauss's law for magnetism can be shown in two ways: one is called the "differential form," and the other is the "integral form." These two ways of showing the law mean the same thing. This law is also called "absence of free magnetic poles." Some sources say it has no special name. In another context, this law is known as the "transversality requirement," which means that for waves moving in a plane, the direction of the magnetic field must be perpendicular to the direction the wave travels.
glynde can refer to several places in Germany.
Fabien Eboussi Boulaga was born on January 17, 1934, and died on October 13, 2018. He was a philosopher from Cameroon.

Michael Francis McCormack, born on August 2, 1964, is an Australian politician. He has been the leader of the National Party and the deputy prime minister of Australia since February 2018. McCormack is also in charge of infrastructure, transport, and regional development. Previously, from 2017 to 2018, he was the minister for defense personnel and minister for veterans' affairs. He has been a member of the House of Representatives since 2010, representing the Riverina area in New South Wales. Before politics, McCormack worked as a newspaper editor.

Eldorado is a city in Saline County, Illinois, United States. In 2010, the city's population was 4,122. Its population was highest in 1980, with 5,198 people. The city's name, spelled Eldorado, might have originally been "elderedo" or "elder-redo." This name combines the last names of the town's founders: Judge Samuel Elder, his son William, grandson Francis Marion, and neighbor Joseph Reed, as well as his brother William. Legend says a signpainter for the railroad wrote "Eldorado" on the train depot. This spelling and pronunciation, "el-do-ray-doh," stuck. Eldorado is part of the Illinois–Indiana–Kentucky tri-state area. It is also a bedroom community in the Harrisburg micropolitan statistical area.

Vellum is a material made from animal skin, often used for writing or printing. Another term for it is parchment. Vellum specifically comes from calfskin and is of higher quality than regular parchment. It can be used to make single pages, scrolls, codices, or books. The term "membrane" is often used today because it’s less confusing. The exact animal and its age are hard to determine without a lab, so "membrane" is preferred. Vellum is usually smooth and durable, but quality varies. Making vellum involves cleaning, bleaching, stretching the skin on a frame, and scraping it with a special knife. The process includes alternating between wetting, drying, and scraping to create tension. A final finish may be added by using pumice and a preparation of lime or chalk. Modern "paper vellum" is made from synthetic materials and is called that because it looks and is used like traditional vellum. Paper vellum is used for tracing, technical drawings, plans, and blueprints.

Bihar Muslims are people from the Indian state of Bihar who follow Islam. Most Bihar Muslims are Sunni. Before the Mughal period, all religious leaders, like ulemas and sufis, were Sunni. However, there are also Shia Muslims in Patna. These Shia Muslims are descendants of people who moved from Lucknow in the 1800s.

Morehouse Parish is in Louisiana, U.S. In 2010, it had 27, 979 people. The main town is Bastrop. Morehouse Parish was created in 1844. It is part of the Bastrop, LA Micropolitan Statistical Area and is included in the Monroe–Ruston–Bastrop, LA Combined Statistical Area.

The Virginia Plan was a proposal for a new national government with three branches and a bicameral legislature. James Madison wrote it while waiting for enough people to join the 1787 Constitutional Convention. This plan was important because it started the main topics of debate. It suggested that more people in a state meant more representatives in the government. This helped larger states. The New Jersey Plan was created to protect smaller states.
Johnny Rozsa is a photographer based in New York. He takes pictures of fashion, people, and famous people.
Bud Brown can mean:

Marina Abramović, born on November 30, 1946, is a Serbian artist. She makes conceptual and performance art, is involved in philanthropy, and creates films about art. Her work looks at the body, how performers connect with audiences, the body's limits, and the mind's possibilities. Active for more than 40 years, Abramović calls herself the "grandmother of performance art." She started involving observers and focused on "dealing with pain, blood, and the body's physical limits."

Sharsheeret is a nonprofit group that helps Jewish women with breast cancer and ovarian cancer. They provide healthcare information, money support, community help, and learning programs to many women and their families in the United States. Sharsheeret has offices in California, Florida, Illinois, New Jersey, and New York. Their main office is in Teaneck, New Jersey. They mainly help young women and Jewish families, as Ashkenazi Jews are more likely to have a BRCA gene change. But they also help people from other backgrounds.

The term "orient" means "east." It traditionally includes countries in the eastern part of the world, as seen from Europe. It is the opposite of "occident," which refers to the western part of the world. In English, "orient" often refers to Asia. This continent is divided into near east, middle east, and far east, which include regions like West Asia, South Asia, East Asia, and Southeast Asia. At first, "orient" meant near east, but its meaning later expanded to include middle east and far east. People often use "oriental" to describe things from the orient. However, in North American English, some people find "oriental" offensive when used to describe people from East Asia or Southeast Asia, as it has eurocentric meanings and its definition has changed over time.

Go-Ahead London is the name used together for all the bus services in London by the Go-Ahead Group. This name started in August 2008. Before that, the company used different names and brands. Go-Ahead London is the biggest bus company in London. It runs 115 bus routes to help Transport for London move people around.

Hurricane Gloria was the first big storm to hit the northeastern United States since Hurricane Agnes in 1972, and the first major storm to hit New York City and Long Island since Hurricane Donna in 1960. It formed in the Atlantic Ocean and became a strong hurricane in September 1985. Gloria moved towards the United States and hit North Carolina on September 27. It then made landfall on Long Island and Connecticut on the same day. The storm weakened and turned into an extratropical storm over New England on September 28. Before hitting land, Gloria caused many people to evacuate, and it was called the "storm of the century." Strong winds stayed to the east of the center, sparing some areas. However, hurricanes brought down trees and power lines, leaving over 4 million people without power, including the worst power outage in Connecticut's history. On Long Island, 1.5 million people were affected. Fallen trees caused six of the fourteen storm-related deaths. In North Carolina, high waves damaged homes and caused heavy beach erosion. High waves also damaged piers, boats, and docks in the mid-Atlantic states. Flooding closed several highways, and thousands in Pennsylvania had to leave their homes. The storm surge destroyed 48 homes on Long Island, and many more had damaged roofs. Crop damage was about $20 million. Overall, damage in the United States was estimated at $900 million, less than expected. In Canada, Gloria's remnants caused minor power outages in New Brunswick, and confusion about the storm led to the creation of the Canadian Hurricane Centre.

Colusa, formerly known as Colusi, Colusi's, Koru, and Salmon Bend, is the county seat of Colusa County, California. In 2010, the population was 5,971, an increase from 5,402 in 2000. Colusi comes from the local Coru Native American tribe, who lived on the other side of the Sacramento River in the 1840s.
This list includes NHL players who have played at least one game from 1917 to now and have last names starting with "S". The list was last updated for the 2018–19 NHL season.

Student transport involves taking children and teenagers to and from school and school events. They can walk, ride a bike, or even use a horse. Older students might drive. Family members or caregivers can also go with them. Alternatively, buses or taxis can be used for group transport.

The Shaolin monastery, also called the Shaolin temple, is a Chan (zen) Buddhist temple in Dengfeng county, Henan province, China. It is thought to have been founded in the fifth century. The Shaolin temple is the main temple of the Shaolin school of Buddhism today. It is located west of Zhengzhou city. The Shaolin monastery and its pagoda forest became a UNESCO World Heritage site in 2010 as part of the "Historic Monuments of Dengfeng".

The Yakovlev Yak-18 is a military training plane. It has two seats in a row and was made in the Soviet Union. It originally used one 119 kilowatt (160 horsepower) Shvetsov M-11FR-1 engine. It started being used in 1946. A version was also made in China as the Nanchang CJ-5.

Edward Paul Abbey was an American writer who lived from January 29, 1927, to March 14, 1989. He wrote about protecting the environment and criticized how public lands were managed. His famous book, "The Monkey Wrench Gang," inspired environmental and eco-terrorist groups. He also wrote a non-fiction book called "Desert Solitaire."

Pärnu is the fourth largest city in Estonia. Tallinn, the capital city, is north of Pärnu. Tartu, Estonia's second largest city, is to the east. Pärnu is in southwestern Estonia, on the coast of Pärnu Bay, which is part of the Gulf of Riga in the Baltic Sea. It is a popular summer holiday place with many hotels, restaurants, and big beaches. The Pärnu River runs through the city and empties into the Gulf of Riga. Pärnu had an airport.

The national flag of Singapore was adopted in 1959, the year Singapore became self-governing. It was officially confirmed again when Singapore separated from Malaysia on August 9, 1965. Before becoming independent, it was the only flag in Malaysia without a 1:2 size ratio. The flag has two colors, red on top and white below. In the top left corner, there is a white crescent moon and a five-pointed star. The crescent moon and star symbolize a young nation on the rise. The red and white colors stand for universal brotherhood and equality. The stars represent national ideals. On the sea, ships do not use the national flag as their main flag. Instead, merchant ships and pleasure boats fly a different flag with a red background and a crescent and star emblem in the middle. Government ships like coast guard vessels fly a blue flag with the national flag in the top left corner and an eight-pointed compass in the bottom part. Warships fly a similar flag but in white with a red compass emblem. There are rules about when and how to fly the flag. Now, citizens can display it from their vehicles during holidays and from their homes at any time.

The highest level of college sports in the U.S. is called NCAA Division I (D-I). D-I schools have big budgets, fancy facilities, and give out more athletic scholarships compared to Division II and III schools. They also compete in the highest level of intercollegiate sports. D-I used to be called the University Division before 1973, when they changed to numeric divisions. The University Division became Division I, while the College Division split into Division II and Division III. For football, D-I schools are divided into three groups: FBS, FCS, and non-football schools. FBS teams need more people to watch their games and give out more scholarships. FCS teams don’t have these requirements. In 2014-15, 345 of the 1,066 NCAA schools were in Division I. Of these, 125 were in FBS, 125 in FCS, and 95 had no football team. Six schools were moving from Division II to Division I. Schools can’t move to Division I until 2012. Now, if a school wants to move to Division I, it must join a conference and show the NCAA it can support a Division I program financially.

Varduhi Varderesyan was an Armenian actress. She moved to Armenia in 1946 and finished her studies at the Leninakan Drama Theatre School (now in Gyumri, Armenia). She then worked at the same theater. Since 1958, she was a leading actress at the Sundukyan Drama Theatre in Yerevan. In 1988, she became a People's Artist of the USSR. In 2002, she was named an honorary citizen of Yerevan.
Tjako van Schie was born on April 17, 1961, in Coevorden. He is a Dutch pianist and composer. He works as a répétiteur at the Amsterdam Conservatory.

Gladys Constance Cooper, born on December 18, 1888, and died on November 17, 1971, was an English actress. Her career lasted for seven decades, appearing in plays, films, and television. As a teenager, she acted in Edwardian musicals and silent films before World War I. From 1917 to 1933, she managed the Playhouse Theatre and performed in many roles there. In the 1920s, she was praised for her performances in plays by W. Somerset Maugham. In the 1930s, she starred in productions in London and Broadway. Cooper moved to Hollywood in 1940 and had success in various character roles. She received three Academy Award nominations for Best Supporting Actress: for "The Song of Bernadette" in 1943, "My Fair Lady" in 1964, and most famously for "Now, Voyager" in 1942. Throughout the 1950s and 1960s, she continued working on both stage and screen, her last stage performance was in her final year.

The mystery of Anna, also called Anna: The Story of Anna, is a 1986 TV movie. It was made in America, Austria, and Italy. The film was directed by Marvin J. Chomsky. Stars in the movie include Amy Irving, Rex Harrison (his last film), Olivia de Havilland, Omar Sharif, Christian Bale (his first film), and Jan Niklas. The movie is based on the story of Grand Duchess Anastasia Nikolaevna of Russia and a book called "The Riddle of Anna and Anna Anderson" by Peter Kurth. It was shown in two parts originally.

Stanisław Karczewski was born on November 14, 1955, in Warsaw. He is a Polish politician and surgeon. Karczewski has been a senator since 2005. He was deputy marshal of the senate from 2011 to 2015. He became marshal of the senate from 2019 to 2015, and then again from 2019.

Aldgate is a London Underground station near Aldgate in the City of London. It is on the Circle Line between other stations, and is the eastern end of the Metropolitan Line. Aldgate is in Travelcard Zone 1. It opened in 1876 with its entrance on Aldgate High Street. An adjacent station, Aldgate East, opened eight years later. Today, Aldgate East is served by the District and Hammersmith & City Lines.
Struth is a commune in Haut-Rhin department, which is in Alsace, a region in northeastern France.

The Equality Act 2010 is a law in the United Kingdom that aims to bring together, update, and add to many older laws about stopping discrimination. These older laws include the Equal Pay Act 1970, the Sex Discrimination Act 1975, the Race Relations Act 1976, the Disability Discrimination Act 1995, and laws protecting people based on religion, sexual orientation, and age. This new law has similar goals to EU equal treatment rules but also offers more protection. It stops discrimination based on nationality and citizenship, and covers more areas of life than just work. It protects people from unfair treatment, harassment, and being targeted because of their age, disability, gender, marriage, pregnancy, race, religion, sex, or sexual orientation. The law allows single-sex services if it is fair. For people with disabilities, employers and service providers must make their workplaces better to help disabled people. This didn't change the rules, but it was already required by other laws. In Northern Ireland, this law doesn't apply in most cases, except for some situations.
Dawson County is in Montana, a state in the U.S. In 2010, it had 8, 966 people. The county seat is Glendive.

Edward Reed Jr., born on September 11, 1978, was a safety in the NFL. He played most of his career with the Baltimore Ravens. Reed was a two-time All-American in college football at the University of Miami. He was drafted by the Ravens in 2002 and played for them for 11 seasons before joining the Houston Texans and New York Jets in 2013. During his career, Reed was picked for nine Pro Bowls and won the 2004 NFL Defensive Player of the Year award. He holds the NFL record for the longest interception return, with 107 yards in 2008. Reed also had a record 1,590 interception return yards and nine postseason interceptions. His 64 regular-season interceptions were among the top 10 in NFL history when he retired. Reed was known as a "ball hawk" and was very good at studying film to predict opposing teams' plays. He was also skilled at making quarterbacks throw interceptions. Reed was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2019. After retiring, Reed became a coach. He worked as an assistant defensive backs coach for the Buffalo Bills in 2016. In 2020, he became the chief of staff for the Miami Hurricanes football team.
No fun at all, often abbreviated to NFAA, is a Swedish punk rock band.

Michael Rennie, born Eric Alexander Rennie, was an actor from Britain. He is most famous for playing the space visitor Klaatu in the 1951 science fiction movie "The Day the Earth Stood Still." He acted in films and on television for over 30 years and was in more than 50 movies.

An illuminated manuscript has decorated text, like gold or silver initials, borders, and small pictures. It usually means any decorated or illustrated book from Western traditions. Eastern and Mesoamerican works are called painted instead. Islamic manuscripts might be called illuminated, illustrated, or painted, using similar techniques to Western works. The earliest known illuminated manuscripts date from 400 to 600 AD, made in the Ostrogothic and Eastern Roman kingdoms. They were important because they helped keep literacy alive. Without them, many ancient Greek and Roman texts might have been lost. These manuscripts were mostly religious, but from the 13th century, more non-religious texts were illustrated. Most surviving manuscripts are from the Middle Ages, with some from the Renaissance and a few from late antiquity. Most were religious, but as time went on, more non-religious texts were decorated. Most were written on parchment, usually from calf, sheep, or goat skin. Some were written on vellum, the highest quality parchment. By the late Middle Ages, manuscripts were sometimes written on paper. Early printed books sometimes had spaces for decorations, but printing quickly reduced the need for hand-illuminated manuscripts. By the early 16th century, they were made in smaller numbers, mostly for the wealthy. These manuscripts are common survivors from the Middle Ages, with many thousands still existing. They are the best examples of medieval painting and are well-preserved. In fact, they are often the only surviving paintings from certain areas and times.

The turnip, also known as the white turnip (Brassica rapa subsp. rapa), is a root vegetable. It is grown in many places with cool climates for its white, fleshy root. The word "turnip" comes from "turn" meaning rounded, and "neep," which comes from the Latin word "napus" for the plant. Smaller, tender turnips are eaten by people, while larger ones are used to feed animals. In some areas of England, Scotland, Ireland, Cornwall, and parts of Canada, "turnip" or "neep" can also mean rutabaga. Rutabaga is a bigger, yellow root vegetable in the same plant family (Brassica) and is also called swede, from "Swedish turnip."

The Butler (full title Lee Daniels' The Butler) is a 2013 American movie about history. Lee Daniels directed and co-produced it, with Danny Strong writing the screenplay. The movie is based on a Washington Post article by Wil Haygood. Set in the White House, the film follows the life of Eugene Allen, played by Forest Whitaker. Whitaker is an African-American butler who worked there for 34 years and witnessed important political and social events in the 20th century. The movie also stars Oprah Winfrey, John Cusack, Jane Fonda, and other famous actors. This was the last film produced by Laura Ziskin, who passed away on June 12, 2011. The movie was first shown in theaters on August 16, 2013. Critics mostly liked the movie, praising the actors but pointing out some inaccuracies in how President Reagan was portrayed. The film earned more than $176 million worldwide, with a budget of $30 million.

Highlands is a town in Orange County, New York, United States. It is located on the eastern part of the county. According to the 2010 census, the population was 12,492. To the west, you can find West Point, which includes the United States Military Academy. The military reservation takes up a large part of the town and is next to the Hudson River.

Mr. Men is a series of children's books by Roger Hargreaves, starting in 1971. Each book introduces a different character with a single personality trait to teach a simple lesson. In 1981, Little Miss books were added, with female characters. A series about animals called Timbuctoo began in 1978. After Roger Hargreaves died in 1988, his son Adam Hargreaves wrote new Mr. Men and Little Miss stories. They include characters like Mr. Cool, Mr. Rude, Mr. Good, Little Miss Scary, Little Miss Bad, and Little Miss Whoops. The original Mr. Men and Little Miss series had 85 characters by 2015. The books were very popular, selling over 100 million copies in 28 countries. All the characters come from a town called Tickle Town.
Lion-sur-mer is a town in Calvados, which is in Normandy. Normandy is in northwestern France.
66 is the number that comes right after 65 and before 67. This number is used in many ways.

Timothy Mackenzie Gunn, born on July 29, 1953, is an American fashion consultant, TV personality, actor, voice actor, and author. He taught at Parsons School of Design from 1982 to 2007 and was the chair of fashion design there from August 2000 to March 2007. After that, he worked as the chief creative officer at Liz Claiborne, which is now called Kate Spade & Company. Gunn became famous as a mentor on the TV show "Project Runway" over 16 seasons. His popularity on "Project Runway" led to two spin-off shows: "Tim Gunn's Guide to Style" on Bravo and "Under the Gunn" on Lifetime. He also wrote five books. Besides being an executive producer, Gunn mentored young designers on "Project Runway." He also provided the voice for Baileywick, a character in the Disney Junior show "Sofia the First," and narrated the sitcom "Mixology."
Wilkes County is the name of two counties in the United States.

Stopover is an unincorporated community in Pike County, Kentucky, United States. It is near the junction of Kentucky Route 194 and Kentucky Route 2062, east of Phelps. Stopover had a post office with the ZIP code 41568. The town's name came from its first postmaster, who owned the local general store. He would often tell people to "stop over and see" him. The town has a small country store and four churches: Shepard Memorial Presbyterian Church, Stopover Church of God, Stopover Freewill Baptist Church, and Camp Creek Pentecostal Church.

Antonio de Cabezón was a Spanish composer and organist who lived from 1510 to 1566. He became famous as a performer even though he was blind from childhood. He worked for the royal family. He was one of the most important composers of his time and the first major keyboard composer from Iberia.
Unionville is a city in Appanoose County, Iowa, in the United States. According to the 2010 census, it had 102 people.

John Robert Lewis was an American leader who fought for civil rights. He served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 1987 until he died in 2020. He was a key person in the Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee from 1963 to 1966. Lewis was one of the main leaders at the 1963 March on Washington. He played a big role in the civil rights movement, helping to end segregation in the United States. He was a member of the Democratic Party and first went to Congress in 1986. He served for 17 terms and became an important leader in the U.S. House of Representatives, starting as a chief deputy whip in 1991 and later as senior chief deputy whip in 2003. Lewis received many honors, including the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

A theocracy is a government where a god is seen as the most important leader, giving special guidance to humans who handle daily tasks. In ancient Rome, the imperial cult treated Roman emperors and some family members as having divine authority, called "auctoritas." Offering "cultus" to a living emperor meant accepting his rule as divinely approved. Emperors should show respect to traditional gods and customs.

Edward Vincent Bracken was an American actor born on February 7, 1915, and died on November 14, 2002. He became famous for his comedy roles in Hollywood. He starred in two popular films, "Hail the Conquering Hero" and "The Miracle of Morgan's Creek," both released in 1944. These films are still kept safe in the National Film Registry. During this time, he also performed well on Broadway in plays like "Too Many Girls" in 1939. Later in his career, he appeared in movies such as "National Lampoon's Vacation" in 1983, "Oscar" in 1991, and "Rookie of the Year" in 1993.

The Lexington Barbecue Festival is a one-day food festival in October. It is in Lexington, North Carolina, known as the "barbecue capital of the world." Each year, around 200,000 people visit the uptown area of Lexington to taste foods from about 20 local restaurants, many food vendors, and other vendors. The event is in a book called "1,000 Places to See in the USA & Canada Before You Die," part of a series based on "1,000 Places to See Before You Die." In 2012, U.S. News and World Report ranked Lexington as the 4th best city for barbecue.

Flavio Cotti was born on October 18, 1939, in Prato-Sornico. He is a Swiss politician. Cotti joined the Federal Council of Switzerland on December 10, 1986. He stopped serving on April 30, 1999. He works with the Christian Democratic People's Party of Switzerland. While he was in office, he was the president of the confederation twice, first in 1991, and again in 1998.

Kmfdm, originally called "No pity for the majority," is a German industrial band led by Sascha Konietzko. He started the band in 1984 as a performance art project. The band's first members were German drummer En Esch and British singer Raymond Watts. Watts left and returned several times over the band's history. The band recorded their early albums in Germany. Konietzko and Esch later moved to the U.S., where they became more successful with the label Wax Trax!. In 1990, German guitarist Günter Schulz joined. Schulz and Esch stayed with the band until 1999 when the band broke up. Konietzko revived the band in 2002 with Lucia Cifarelli, Jules Hodgson, Steve White, and Andy Selway. In 2007, Konietzko and Cifarelli moved to Germany, while the others stayed in the U.S. Hodgson and White left between 2015 and 2017, leaving the band a working trio. Over 20 studio albums and two dozen singles, dozens of musicians have worked with the band, selling over two million records worldwide. Critics say kmfdm was one of the first to bring industrial music to mainstream audiences. Konietzko calls their music "the ultra-heavy beat." The band mixes heavy metal guitar riffs, electronic music, samples, and vocals in a variety of styles, including industrial rock and electronic body music. They are politically active, often criticizing violence, war, and oppression in their lyrics. The band tours after major releases and interacts with fans online and at concerts. Members have also recorded under other names like Watts' Pig, Konietzko's Excessive Force, and Esch and Schulz's Slick Idiot.

Alexain is a small town in the Mayenne department, which is in Northwestern France. It is located about 20 km northwest of Laval and 14 km from Mayenne. Its neighboring towns are La Bigottière, Placé, and Saint-Germain-d'Anxure.

Islam Bibi was a female police officer in Afghanistan. She worked in the Helmand province headquarters. She was a leader in fighting for women's rights. At the time of her death, she was the highest-ranking policewoman in Afghanistan. She led operations against the Taliban. She faced many death threats and was killed on July 4, 2013.

The common toad, also known as the European toad, is found across most of Europe (except Ireland, Iceland, and some Mediterranean islands), parts of western Asia, and a small area in northwest Africa. It is one of several similar toads and is part of a species group. During the day, toads are hard to spot as they stay hidden. They become active at dusk and hunt for insects at night. They move slowly and jump short distances, with bumpy, grayish skin. Usually, toads live alone, but during breeding season, many gather at specific ponds. Males compete to mate with females. Eggs are laid in jelly-like strings in the water and hatch into tadpoles. After growing for several months, tadpoles turn into small toads with limbs, a process called metamorphosis. The young toads leave the water and live mostly on land. The common toad seems to be decreasing in some areas, but overall, it's not considered threatened. It faces threats like losing its breeding habitats and being killed on roads during its yearly migrations. Toads have been linked to witchcraft in stories and traditions.

HTC Corporation is a company that makes electronics, based in Xindian, New Taipei City, Taiwan. It was founded in 1997. At first, HTC made laptop computers. Later, they started making smartphones, especially those using Windows Mobile. HTC was one of the first companies to make phones that ran Android. However, because of competition, their market share dropped to 7.2% by April 2015. HTC then faced financial problems and made losses. In 2016, HTC began making virtual reality products, like the HTC Vive. They also worked with Google on making phones. In 2017, HTC sold some of its smartphone design and research talent to Google for a billion dollars.

Tanah Merah MRT station is an above-ground Mass Rapid Transit (MRT) station on the East West Line in Bedok, Singapore. It serves the East West Line and is also the end station for the Changi Airport Branch Line, which is part of the East West Line. Tanah Merah station is near the boundaries of Bedok North and Bedok South planning areas. It is on New Upper Changi Road, between Bedok South Avenue 3 and Tanah Merah Kechil Road. Tanah Merah station has more tracks than most other stations, like Ang Mo Kio. The middle track is used by the Changi Airport Branch Line, which ends at Changi Airport. "Tanah Merah" means "red earth" in Malay, named after the red cliffs seen from the sea, though most are now underwater. Since 2017, the station has an extra code "cg" to help differentiate the main service and the Changi branch, though it's not shown on the signs. In 2019, it was announced that by 2040, Tanah Merah station will be moved to the Thomson-East Coast Line, and the Changi Airport Branch Line will stop operating.

Redhill MRT station is an above-ground mass rapid transit station on the East West Line in Bukit Merah, Singapore. It is on Tiong Bahru Road, at the intersection with Jalan Tiong. On the East West Line, it is between Tiong Bahru and Queenstown stations. The station opened on March 12, 1988, when the MRT line was extended from Outram Park to Clementi.

Los Ángeles is the capital of Bío Bío province, in a place called the same name, in Bío Bío, in Chile's center-south. It sits between the Laja and Biobío rivers. In 2012, it had 186, 671 people. Los Ángeles municipality has the most rural people of any in Chile. North of the city is Laja Falls. About 100 kilometers east is the Antuco volcano in the Andes. Los Ángeles is a starting point for visiting nearby Laguna del Laja national park and the volcano. The city has an airport called María Dolores.

Flushing is a city in Genesee County, Michigan. In 2010, it had 8, 389 people. It is near Flint and considered a suburb. Even though it is in the flushing charter township, it is its own administrative area. Flushing started as a mill town in the mid-1830s. Its location along the Flint River, the county's largest river, was important for settling there. The river's water power was crucial for choosing where to build the town. The area around Flushing was also good for farming. Originally, the town was going to be called Dover, but that name was already used in another part of Michigan. Charles Seymour, who used to live in Flushing, New York, suggested naming the new town after the New York village.

A provincial city, often called a city, is a type of second-level subdivision in Vietnam. There are 713 such units, including urban districts, districts, and towns, which all have the same status. By decree 42/2009/ND-CP, cities are officially divided into class-1, class-2, or class-3. Cities are only found within provinces at the second level. At the third level, cities are divided into wards and communes.

Justin Raimondo, born Dennis Raimondo on November 18, 1951, and died on June 27, 2019, was an American author. He worked as the editorial director of antiwar.com. He called himself a conservative-paleo-libertarian.

Arshile Gorky, born Vostanik Manoug Adoian on April 15, 1904, and died on July 21, 1948, was an Armenian-American painter. He lived most of his life in the United States. Gorky had a big influence on abstract expressionism. Along with Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock, and Willem de Kooning, he is considered one of the most powerful American painters of the 20th century. His paintings were likely inspired by the pain and loss he experienced during the Armenian genocide.

Evan Rachel Wood, born on September 7, 1987, is an American actress, model, and musician. She has won a Critics' Choice Television Award and been nominated for three Primetime Emmy Awards and three Golden Globe Awards for her work in film and television. Wood started acting in the 1990s, appearing in TV shows like "American Gothic" (1995-1996) and "Once and Again" (1999-2002). At nine years old, she starred in "Digging to China" (1997) and was praised for her role as the troubled teenager Tracy Freeland in "Thirteen" (2003). She continued to act in indie films such as "Pretty Persuasion" (2005), "Down in the Valley" (2005), "Running with Scissors" (2006), and the bigger movie "Across the Universe" (2007). Since 2008, Wood has been in mainstream films like "The Wrestler" (2008), "Whatever Works" (2009), and "The Ides of March" (2011). She also acted on TV, playing vampire Sophie-Anne Leclerq in "True Blood" (2009-2011) and the daughter of Mildred Pierce in the HBO series "Mildred Pierce" (2011), for which she was nominated for a Golden Globe and an Emmy for best supporting actress. Wood plays the character Dolores Abernathy, a sentient android, in the HBO series "Westworld" (2016-present), earning a Critics' Choice Award and nominations for a Golden Globe and an Emmy. She also voiced Queen Iduna in the Disney film "Frozen II" (2019).
Marcel Dupré, born on May 3, 1886, and died on May 30, 1971, was a French organist, composer, and teacher.

Burnout Paradise is a 2008 open-world racing game. Criterion Games made it, and Electronic Arts published it for PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, and Windows. It was also available on the PlayStation Store and Xbox Live Marketplace's games on demand. Later, it was added to the Greatest Hits and Platinum Hits collections and became compatible with the Xbox One in November 2016. This was the first Burnout game on Windows. The game is set in a fictional city called Paradise. Players can race in different types of races and compete online, including a "cops and robbers" mode. Updates added a time-of-day cycle and motorcycles. New cars and the fictional "Big Surf Island" were also available as paid downloadable content. It was very popular when it came out. Websites like Gamerankings and Metacritic gave it an 88% score. It won several awards in 2008, including best driving game from Spike TV, GameTrailers, and Gamespot. Reviewers praised its speed and open-world gameplay. A remastered version called Burnout Paradise Remastered was released in 2018 for PlayStation 4, Xbox One, and Windows. Online service for the original game ended in August 2019. A remastered version for Nintendo Switch was released in 2020.

Walter Perry Johnson, nicknamed "Barney" and "The Big Train," was a major league baseball player. He was a right-handed pitcher who played for the Washington Senators for 21 years from 1907 to 1927. Later, he managed the Senators from 1929 to 1932 and the Cleveland Indians from 1933 to 1935. Johnson is often considered one of the best pitchers in baseball history. He set several pitching records that still stand today. He is the all-time leader in shutouts with 110, and he won 417 games, which is second best. He also had 531 complete games, ranking fourth. Johnson held the career strikeout record for nearly 56 years, striking out 3,508 batters. He was the only player in the 3,000 strikeout club until 1974. Johnson led the league in strikeouts 12 times, a record he set by striking out over 400 batters and 3,500 batters in total. He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1976 as one of the "first five" members. Johnson was known for his gentle nature and good sportsmanship, and his name is associated with friendly competition.

Asian Americans are people with Asian ancestry living in America. The term includes many diverse groups from East Asia, South Asia, and Southeast Asia, as defined by the U.S. Census Bureau. This group includes people who identify as "Asian," such as Chinese, Filipino, Indian, Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, and others. In 2018, Asian Americans made up 5.4% of the U.S. population, increasing to 6.5% when including those who are multiracial. Migrants from Asia have been in parts of the U.S. since the 17th century, but large-scale immigration began in the mid-19th century. From the 1880s to the 1920s, laws restricted most Asian immigration. After immigration laws changed in the 1940s and 1960s, Asian immigration increased rapidly. Census data from 2010 show that Asian Americans are the fastest-growing racial or ethnic minority in the United States.

Ali Hassan Mwinyi, born on May 8, 1925, in Kivure, Pwani region, Tanzania, was a Tanzanian politician. He served as the second president of Tanzania from 1985 to 1995. Before becoming president, he was the interior minister and vice president. He was also the chairman of the ruling party, the Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM), from 1990 to 1996. During Mwinyi's presidency, Tanzania began to change its socialist policies started by Julius Nyerere. He made it easier to bring in goods and encouraged private businesses. In his second term, Tanzania allowed more than one political party, pushed by international donors. Mwinyi was often called "Mzee Rukhsa," meaning "everything goes." He supported changes in morals, beliefs, and values, as long as they didn't break the law. Many say that under Mwinyi's leadership, Tanzania moved away from the failed socialist policies that hurt the economy. During his time as president, important decisions were made to open up the economy, leading to better economic growth in the short term.

Samsun is a city on Turkey's north coast. It has about 1.4 million people. Samsun is the capital of Samsun province and a major Black Sea port. The city is growing and has two universities, several hospitals, shopping malls, and a lot of small factories. It also has sports facilities and an opera. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk started the Turkish War of Independence in Samsun in 1919.

Haute-Ajoie is a municipality in the district of Porrentruy, in the canton of Jura, Switzerland. It was created on January 1, 2009, by combining the former municipalities of Chevenez, Damvant, Réclère, and Roche-d'Or. On January 1, 2018, the former municipality of Rocourt joined Haute-Ajoie.
Garden Valley is a town in Jackson County, Wisconsin, United States. The town had 406 people in the 2000 census. North Branch is an unincorporated community in Garden Valley.

The University of Idaho (U of I or UI) is a public research university in Moscow, Idaho. It is the state's land-grant and main research university, and leads the Idaho Space Grant Consortium. For 71 years, until 1963, it was the only university in the state. Its law school, started in 1909, was first accredited by the American Bar Association in 1925. The university began in 1889, opened in 1892, and had 40 students in its first class. The first graduates in 1896 were two men and two women. Now, it has over 12,000 students, mostly on the Moscow campus. U of I offers 142 degree programs, from accounting to wildlife resources, including bachelor's, master's, doctoral, and specialist degrees. They also give certificates in 30 areas of study. It has the highest 4 and 6-year graduation rates among public universities in Idaho, at 25% and 53%, respectively. The university does a lot of research, generating 74% of all research money in the state, with $100 million spent in 2010. As a land-grant university and the main research university, U of I has the biggest campus in the state, in the rolling Palouse hills at over 1,000 feet above sea level. Students play for the Idaho Vandals in NCAA Division I sports. Besides the main Moscow campus, U of I has smaller campuses in Coeur d'Alene, Boise, and Idaho Falls. They also run a research park in Post Falls and many extension offices statewide.

Hurricane Isaac was the last storm of the 2006 Atlantic hurricane season. It began as a tropical wave entering the Atlantic Ocean on September 18. By September 27, it had grown into a tropical depression, southeast of Bermuda. It became a tropical storm the next day. But it couldn't get stronger because of bad weather and cooler water. Isaac became a Category 1 hurricane and came close to Newfoundland as a tropical storm. The effects were small, with just some strong winds, rough waves, and some rain.

The Christian Community is a religious group that thinks of itself as a Christian denomination, but other Christian churches do not recognize it as such. It was started in 1922 in Switzerland by Lutheran theologians and ministers, led by Friedrich Rittelmeyer, who was inspired by Rudolf Steiner, an Austrian philosopher who created anthroposophy. The Christian Community has local groups that are financially independent. These groups are overseen by regional and international administrative bodies. There are about 100,000 members worldwide, and their main headquarters are in Berlin, Germany. The Christian Community is led by a group called the "Circle of Priests." Leaders in this group are known as coordinators. The top coordinator, called the first coordinator, is advised by two second coordinators. There are also third coordinators at the regional level, and a group of priests called the synod.

The International Baccalaureate (IB) is a non-profit organization based in Geneva, Switzerland. It was founded in 1968. IB offers four educational programs: the Diploma Programme and the Career-related Programme for students aged 15 to 19, the Middle Years Programme for students aged 11 to 16, and the Primary Years Programme for children aged 3 to 12. To teach these programs, schools must be authorized by the IB. In 2007, the organization changed its name and logo to better reflect its structure. Now, "IB" can refer to the organization, any of the four programs, or the diplomas or certificates awarded at the end of a program.

A diatonic scale is a seven-note scale with five whole steps and two half steps. The two half steps are usually separated by two or three whole steps. This arrangement ensures all half steps are far apart. For example, in a diatonic scale across two octaves, the half steps are not next to each other. Any seven consecutive natural notes, like C-D-E-F-G-A-B, form a diatonic scale. Modern keyboards have white keys that make up a diatonic scale, but sometimes you need black keys for other scales. A diatonic scale can also be seen as two groups of four notes with a whole step in between. The term "diatonic" comes from ancient Greek music theory. In modern music theory, a diatonic scale has seven notes and meets specific spacing requirements. Other seven-note scales, like harmonic or melodic minor, do not fit these requirements.

The national football team of Ireland represents the country in men's international football. It is managed by the Football Association of Ireland. The team first played in the 1924 Olympics, reaching the quarter-finals. From 1924 to 1936, they were known as the Irish Free State, and from 1936 to 1950, they were called Éire or Ireland. In 1953, FIFA decided that for tournament matches, the team from the Republic of Ireland would be called the Republic of Ireland, while the team from Northern Ireland would be called Northern Ireland. Northern Ireland could still use "Ireland" in home international competitions until 1984. In 1949, the team from the Republic of Ireland defeated England at home for the first time. They also reached the quarter-finals of the 1964 European Nations Cup, losing to Spain. Under Jack Charlton's leadership, the team had its best period. They reached the sixth position in FIFA's world rankings in 1993, qualified for UEFA Euro 1988, and made it to the quarter-finals of the 1990 World Cup for the first time. They also reached the last 16 of the 1994 World Cup. Mick McCarthy took over after Charlton and although they didn't succeed in the next three major tournaments, they qualified for the 2002 World Cup and made it to the quarter-finals. Martin O'Neill continued this success, taking them to the last 16 at UEFA Euro 2016. The team's home stadium is the Aviva Stadium in Dublin, though they play some home games in other stadiums across the country. Stephen Kenny is currently the coach, and Séamus Coleman is the captain.

Antonio Montana is a fictional character and the main hero in the 1983 film "Scarface." Al Pacino acts as Montana in the movie, and André Sogliuzzo voices him in the 2006 video game. Montana's journey from the bottom to the top became a cultural symbol, making him one of the most famous movie characters ever. In 2008, "Empire" magazine ranked him as the 27th greatest movie character. He partly follows the story of Tony Camonte, the main character from the original novel and the 1932 film. Montana is also inspired by Al Capone. Oliver Stone said Montana's last name came from his favorite NFL player, Joe Montana. A prequel novel, "Scarface: The Beginning," was written by L. A. Banks and published in 2006. Montana has a big scar on his face, which is why he is called Scarface.

sea glass and beach glass are similar but come from different types of water. Sea glass is made from glass that has been washed and weathered by the salt water in the sea. This weathering makes it look frosted. Sea glass is often collected as a hobby and used to make pretty jewelry. Beach glass comes from fresh water and looks less frosted than sea glass. Sea glass can take 20 to 40 years, sometimes even 100 years, to become smooth and frosted. This happens because of something called longshore drift, which makes the edges smooth. In everyday use, people often use these terms interchangeably.

Alan Harrison Berg was born on January 1, 1934, and died on June 18, 1984. He was an American lawyer and talk radio host in Denver, Colorado. Berg was known for his liberal views and his direct way of talking on his show. On June 18, 1984, Berg was shot and killed by members of a white nationalist group called the Order. The people who killed him were part of a group planning to hurt important Jewish people, including Berg. Two of them, David Lane and Bruce Pierce, were found guilty of violating civil rights, but not for murder. They were sentenced to 190 years and 252 years in prison, respectively.

Balltown is a city in Dubuque County, Iowa, United States. It is in the Dubuque, Iowa, metropolitan area. The population was 68 in 2010, down from 73 in 2000. Balltown has a restaurant called Breitbach's Country Dining, which is Iowa's oldest and was founded in 1852. The restaurant was rebuilt twice by the community after it was destroyed by fire in 2007 and 2008.

Ell is a small town in western Luxembourg, near the border with Belgium. It is part of a commune in the canton of Redange. The town of Ell has 340 people. Other towns in the commune are Colpach-bas, Colpach-haut, and Roodt.

Tabaré Ramón Vázquez Rosas, born on January 17, 1940, is a Uruguayan politician. He was the 41st president of Uruguay from 2015 to 2020. Earlier, he served as the 39th president from 2005 to 2010. A doctor specializing in oncology, Vázquez is part of the leftist Broad Front coalition. He first became president in October 2004, took office in March 2005, and left in March 2010. José Mujica succeeded him as president from 2010 to 2015. Vázquez was elected again in 2015 and finished his term in 2020, when Luis Alberto Lacalle Pou became the new president.

A volcanic plug is formed when magma hardens inside a volcano's vent. If rising magma is trapped below it, pressure builds up and can cause an explosive eruption. Erosion by glaciers can expose the plug on one side, leaving a slope on the other. This creates a landform called a crag and tail. If the plug is protected, erosion might remove the surrounding rock, leaving the plug standing alone, creating a unique landform.

Saint Kitts and Nevis, officially known as the Federation of Saint Christopher and Nevis, is a small island country in the West Indies. It is part of the Leeward Islands in the Lesser Antilles. Saint Kitts and Nevis is the smallest independent country in the Western Hemisphere by both size and population. It is a commonwealth realm, with Queen Elizabeth II as the head of state. The capital, Basseterre, is on the larger island of Saint Kitts. Nevis, the smaller island, is southeast of Saint Kitts. Anguilla, a British dependency, used to be part of this area but separated and is now a British overseas territory. To the north and northeast are Antigua and Barbuda, and to the southeast is the small uninhabited island of Redonda (part of Antigua and Barbuda) and Montserrat. Saint Kitts and Nevis were among the first Caribbean islands to be colonized by Europeans. Saint Kitts was home to the first British and French colonies in the Caribbean and is known as "the mother colony of the West Indies." It gained independence in 1983.
